#7804. Three men charged in $130M AI impersonation scheme

Three foreign nationals are accused of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million. (Image from Shutterstock)

Federal prosecutors in Manhattan have unsealed an indictment accusing three foreign nationals of using artificial intelligence to pose as corporate executives and lawyers in a fraud scheme that allegedly took in over $129 million, according a story published Friday in The Guardian.

According to the U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York, Jacob Soall, Sharon Hazan and Guy Sheetrit manipulated voices and images to deceive employees at companies around the world between 2024 and 2026. Soall and Hazan were arrested in Spain this summer, and Sheetrit was taken into custody in the United Kingdom in September.

According to prosecutors, the scheme worked in two stages. First, the defendants allegedly posed as a company executive and told employees they needed help with a confidential financial matter. Employees were then directed to contact attorneys at a major international law firm, whom the defendants also allegedly impersonated, and to wire large sums as instructed.

Prosecutors allege that the defendants stole nearly $5 million from a Missouri hospital system, about $2.7 million from a Rhode Island bank, roughly $3 million from a California hospital system, more than $4.6 million from a Massachusetts mutual fund, about $5 million from a Florida pet food company, and over $11 million from a U.K. technology company. The defendants have been indicted on charges relating to wire fraud, money laundering, conspiracy and identity theft.

Funds were allegedly routed to accounts in countries including the U.S., Spain, Portugal, Greece, the United Arab Emirates, Singapore, Austria, Slovakia and China, then converted to cryptocurrency to hide their origin and split among conspirators. Prosecutors say Soall and Hazan used several aliases, including “Rocky Balboa,” “Superman Cash” and “Ron.”

U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald said in a statement that while AI holds great promise, it can also be turned to criminal ends.

#7803. Ukrainian National Sentenced for Role in Hacking Hospitals, Businesses, and Governments as Part of Ransomware Conspiracies Causing Over $100 Million in Losses

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Artem Stryzhak, 36, a Ukrainian national, was sentenced today to 70 months in prison for conspiracy to commit computer fraud in connection with a series of ransomware attacks that targeted hospitals, government entities, law firms, and other businesses around the world.

“This sentence concludes a years-long, multi-continent investigation into a defendant who participated in cyber-attacks against Americans’ businesses and health care,” said Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva of the Justice Department’s Criminal Division. “Cybercriminals who terrorize American businesses cannot evade justice by operating from abroad or hiding behind sophisticated technology. Artem Stryzhak’s sentence underscores the Justice Department’s resolve to dismantle ransomware groups, hold them accountable, and protect American businesses and people from cyber extortion.”

“Ransomware attacks like those committed by the defendant wreak enormous havoc — harming victim companies that pay millions in remediation and ransoms, preventing hospitals and other critical facilities from accessing data, and putting sensitive information in the hands of bad actors,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “Today’s sentence reflects that cybercriminals cannot hide from law enforcement and will face significant punishment for their criminal conduct. We remain determined to capture Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, a serial ransomware developer and Stryzhak’s co-conspirator.”

“Disrupting a ransomware group that attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide and sentencing a defendant who had targeted healthcare during the COVID-19 pandemic is of significant importance to this office,” said U.S. Attorney Gregory W. Kehoe for the Middle District of Florida. “We are proud of our law enforcement partners for their skilled investigative work in bringing this criminal to justice.”

“Artem Stryzhak is a prolific cybercriminal who worked with multiple ransomware groups to target U.S. businesses and hospitals,” said Operations Director Brett Leatherman of the FBI’s Cyber Branch. “These groups disrupted patient care and caused more than $100 million in losses. Today’s sentence reflects the seriousness of Stryzhak’s crimes and demonstrates the FBI’s global reach and extensive network of international partners. Multiple field offices contributed to this investigation, and our work does not end here. We will continue to leverage every tool at our disposal to track down Stryzhak’s co-conspirators and hold them accountable, including Volodymyr Viktorovych Tymoshchuk.”

According to court documents, Stryzhak, formerly of Barcelona, Spain, conspired with others to perpetrate ransomware attacks on behalf of multiple ransomware groups against victim computer networks in the United States and other countries. The conspiracies caused significant damage to victim computer systems. Beginning in approximately June 2021, Stryzhak joined the ongoing Nefilim conspiracy as a Nefilim ransomware affiliate.  Stryzhak was given access to the Nefilim ransomware and agreed with one of the Nefilim ransomware group administrators, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk, to pay the Nefilim administrators, including Tymoshchuk, 20% of the ransom proceeds extorted from victims in exchange for Stryzhak’s access to the Nefilim ransomware.

The ransomware attacks that Stryzhak conducted with Nefilim ransomware included a June 2021 attack in which Stryzhak stole data from a company in the oil and gas transportation industry. About a week later, Stryzhak created email addresses that were incorporated in a ransom note sent to the victim company. Stryzhak conspired with the Nefilim ransomware actors until at least October 2021. If a victim paid the ransom demand, the perpetrators provided the decryption key, enabling the victim to decrypt files locked by the ransomware.

Also according to court documents, Stryzhak separately joined the Hive ransomware group as one of its earliest affiliates. From June 2021 to January 2023, Hive conspirators attacked approximately 1,500 victims worldwide, including government entities, hospitals, and businesses. Hive ransomware attacks caused major disruptions in victim daily operations around the world and affected responses to the COVID-19 pandemic. In one case, a hospital attacked by the Hive ransomware group had to forgo digital technology to treat existing patients and was unable to accept new patients immediately following the attack.

In his role as a Hive affiliate, Stryzhak and his co-conspirators deployed Hive ransomware against seven victims, including law firms, a dentist office, and a healthcare provider during the COVID-19 pandemic. Victims were unable to access their encrypted data. The FBI, as part of a months-long disruption campaign against the Hive ransomware group, provided a decryption key to one of Stryzhak’s victims, thereby allowing that victim to decrypt its encrypted data without having to pay a ransom.

Stryzhak was arrested in Spain in June 2024 and extradited to the United States in April 2025. Stryzhak pleaded guilty in December 2025 to two counts of conspiracy to commit fraud, extortion, and related activity in connection with computers.

The FBI Springfield Field Office investigated the Nefilim ransomware case and the FBI Tampa Field Office investigated the Hive ransomware case. The Criminal Division’s Office of International Affairs, the FBI’s New York Field Office, and Spanish law enforcement authorities provided substantial assistance locating, arresting, and extraditing Stryzhak.

Acting Assistant Deputy Chief James S. Yoon of the Criminal Division’s Computer Crime and Intellectual Property Section (CCIPS), former CCIPS Senior Trial Attorney Brian Z. Mund, and Assistant United States Attorneys Alexander F. Mindlin and Ellen H. Sise of the Eastern District of New York’s National Security and Cybercrime Section prosecuted the Nefilim ransomware case. CCIPS Trial Attorneys Alison M. Zitron and Christen M. Gallagher and Assistant United States Attorney Hannah Watson of the Middle District of Florida prosecuted the Hive ransomware case.

The U.S. Department of State’s Transnational Organized Crime (TOC) Rewards Program has offered a reward of up to $11 million for information leading to the arrest and/or conviction or location of Stryzhak’s charged co-conspirator, Volodymyr Tymoshchuk. Anyone with information about Tymoshchuk should contact the FBI via phone at +1-917-242-1407, by email at TymoTips@fbi.gov, by contacting your local field office, if in the United States, or by contacting the nearest U.S. Embassy, if located overseas. More information about the Tymoshchuk TOC reward offer and one related to Hive ransomware is located on the State Department website.

CCIPS investigates and prosecutes cybercrime and intellectual property (IP) crime in coordination with domestic and international law enforcement agencies, often with assistance from the private sector. Since 2020, CCIPS has secured the conviction of over 180 cyber and IP criminals, and court orders for the return of over $350 million in victim funds.

#7802. Back At The Mayflower

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

The first day of the 2026 Federalist Society Convention is in the can. There is much to report.

First, it is good to be back at the Mayflower--well at least good for those of us who made it in. Several years ago, FedSoc decided to move from the Mayflower to the Hilton, a much larger venue. The group had simply outgrown the classic hotel. The downside, of course, is that the Hilton is a terrible hotel. There were assassination attempts on two Presidents at the "Hinkley Hilton." There was no common meeting area, and attendees had to traverse a labyrinth of hallways between sessions. Worse, the rooms were a decade overdue for renovation. We hated it. But most of us were able to fit in.

This year, the registration for the national convention filled up almost instantaneously. I had planned to bring many of my students, but they simply never made it off the waiting list. Longtime members were hanging out in the lobby, hoping to make it off the waiting list, with no luck. I heard that the Harvard FedSoc chapter scheduled a conference for students who could not get in--apparently known as the "shadow docket." People complained to me, as if it was my fault we went back to the small Mayflower because of my carping about the Hilton. I get blamed for everything.

FedSoc will have to figure out what to do for next year, the 40th Anniversary of the National Lawyers Convention. We could always try to check out the new East Wing Ballroom, assuming Judge Leon doesn't enjoin it! The Gaylord Hotel in Maryland could fit everyone, but I am still scarred from the gala dinner there in 2016. I have long been a fan of holding the convention outside of D.C. It would send the exact right message. The times where people in D.C. offices can just stop by for a few panels are long gone. (The sold out registration means only those willing to attend the entire program will be there.) And anyone who wants to speak on the program of this platform should be willing to get on a flight. I would have recommended Texas for the venue, but we will soon be in hostile territory. Perhaps the free state of Florida is the last, best hope.

Second, the format of the FedSoc conference is different. I was so accustomed to the usual rhythm, I feel a bit disoriented. There are no breakout panels. Every panel is a "showcase" panel in the Grand Ballroom. The other rooms are overflow rooms with screens to watch the programming. The schedule is all different. The Rosenkranz Debate was on Thursday afternoon rather than Saturday afternoon over lunch. The Bork and Olson Lectures are both on Friday. And the program ends on Saturday at 2:15, about three hours earlier than usual. Also, instead of having lunchtime panels, all of the rooms on the second floor host smaller, intimate lunches. You could sit at a table with a judge and eight others to chat about an interesting topic. I was at Chief Judge Elrod's table to learn about the Lord of the Rings. (Trigger warning for commenters: I have never read any of those books, I fell asleep during the first movie, and never watched the others.) The discussion was fun! There are some judges who treat their judicial sinecures like Gollum treats the ring. How precious.

I see pros and cons to the new format. On the plus side, this format was far less overwhelming. I routinely felt drained by all of the content. Also, I always felt like I was missing something when I committed to a panel. As a result, I would often bounce between different panels, ensuring that I missed stuff. On the negative side, I enjoyed the ability to pick different panels that may be of interest. I thought the practice groups put on a wide arrange of topical panels. Moreover, there are far fewer speaking slots available with only a few panels each day. These are prime opportunities for up-and-coming members. Still, for this America 250 celebration, I liked the theme in which each panel was framed around a few words from the Declaration. This is an area I have studied for years, and I still learned quite a lot. I don't think we could have kept the Declaration theme going with breakouts.

Third, there is a much stronger focus on students--the lifeblood of Fedsoc. I appreciated that each panel was introduced by a student, rather than the chair of the practice group. During the Scalia dinner, the winners of the Feddie student chapter awards were asked to stand up. I am so proud of the South Texas Chapter, and my students Ryan Lanier and Makayla Arthur, for winning the Hamilton Award for "Most Improved Chapter." Matthew Weinberg, the President of the UCLA chapter during the Percival protest, was given a courage award. And each of the Soc! lunchtime tables was hosted by a student chapter leader.

We can never forget that FedSoc was founded by a bunch of law students. Old people (present company included) need to always give the youth these sorts of opportunities. It wasn't that long ago that I met Will Scharf at the Mayflower, and now he is White House Counsel. I can say the same for so many current judges and other officials that I met when I was student. Indeed, some of the current judges hosted me as a Professor at their chapters! (In 2033, I'll be 49.)  Everything that rises must converge.

Fourth, the decoration of the Mayflower and the Marriott Marquis ballroom was top-notch. There is red, white, and blue bunting all over the Grand Ballroom. The backdrop of the Scalia dinner was expertly done, topped off with George Washington's bible! (No, we couldn't touch it.) The Marine Corp band played during the processional. The Madison Club reception was no longer crammed into a tiny, dark, and noisy tent. It was held in a spacious atrium at the Marquis. Moreover, Madison Club members have access to Edgar's as a lounge to get food and snacks during the day. What a really, really smart idea. This sort of attention to detail matters, at least to me.

Fifth the security is intense. Registration is now available on the lower level. No one is allowed into the hallway without showing credentials and passing through a body scanner. Large bags are banned and smaller bags are searched. The busses from the Mayflower to the Marquis were swept for security, and there was a National Guardsman on board. It is a sad commentary that we have to take these precautions. But with an actual assassination attempt against Justice Kavanaugh, I think we have to accept these costs. (During the Scalia Dinner, Justice Alito praised the courage of Justices Kavanaugh and Barrett for joining the Dobbs decision, knowing what risks that could bring.)

Sixth, I was sort of expecting the vibe at the Mayflower to be grim in light of last week's election. I remember how the 2008 convention felt something like a funeral. I think the mood was mostly one of shock. There are efforts in play to figure out how to deal with the loss of Attorneys General in Texas, Ohio, Iowa, and Kansas. Other states will have to pick up the heavy lifting. Lawyers in Austin can find safe refuge in Baton Rouge, Jackson, St. Louis, Nashville, Tallahassee, Montgomery, and other cities. I am currently researching the laws of intervention on both the plaintiff and defendant side, confessions of error in criminal cases, as well as standing for state legislators and the state senate. The agenda has shifted.

Seventh, one thing I love about the National Convention is that business is conducted right in the hallways. There is a strong sentiment to do everything we can to confirm the remaining judges. These aren't quite the midnight judges of the outgoing Federalist Party, but we are in a similar mindset. There is a universal agreement that Judge Rudofsky was screwed. I second everything my friend Rob Luther wrote in this op-ed in the Arkansas newspaper. And there is a concerted effort to help Elliot Gaiser get across the finish line. What a complete waste if this seat is left for James Talarico to fill. Talk about cutting off your nose to spite your six-gendered face. And then there's Todd Butler. Had the election turned out differently, things may have gone differently. But he is on the path to confirmation. I hope Butler proves me wrong--and he will have a quick opportunity to do so. The January en banc siting has a huge 922(g) case and a challenge to Texas's social media law. As for the new Eighth Circuit nominee, Cody Hiland, he have to prove a lot of people wrong.

#7801. Wells Fargo faces labor board complaint over union vote

The National Labor Relations Board alleged the lender threatened and retaliated against workers in favor of unionization at a California branch.

The National Labor Relations Board has accused Wells Fargo of illegally threatening and retaliating against employees and coercing workers to prevent fair unionization votes at a California branch.

Most employees of an Atwater, California, branch who signed cards supporting unionization in December 2023 voted against unionization the following month, a regional director of the NLRB alleged, in a complaint filed Feb. 11 and seen by Bloomberg,

The NLRB claims Wells Fargo coerced workers to vote against unionization. Wells Fargo has denied that allegation.

The labor board wants the bank to recognize and negotiate with the union despite the vote, based on a 2023 precedent case. The 2023 Cemex ruling strengthened the NLRB's power to compel companies that violate labor laws to recognize unions.

However, Republicans and business groups oppose the precedent. The acting general counsel of NLRB, William Cowen, or his permanent replacement, could withdraw, amend, or settle the Wells Fargo complaint.

President Donald Trump appointed Cowen acting general counsel this month, days after firing NLRB’s previous chief lawyer Jennifer Abruzzo, a Biden appointee, and Democratic board member Gwynne Wilcox.

The email notifying Wilcox of her termination said she was being fired since she did not “share the objectives” of the present administration. Wilcox’s ouster has left the board with only two members coupled with existing vacancies and does not meet the minimum number of members needed to adjudicate routine cases.

Wilcox is suing Trump, alleging the president surpassed his authority in firing her and requesting that she be allowed to resume her work as an NLRB member.

The NLRB complaint does not signify a complete investigation or a full adjudication of the allegations; rather, the regional office found that the allegations may be sufficient to go to a hearing to consider all evidence and make credibility determinations, a Wells Fargo spokesperson noted.

Employees at the Atwater branch voted 3-1 to reject unionization in January 2024. The branch manager allegedly told staff she knew about organizing discussions and warned about camera surveillance. She also reportedly told workers that Wells Fargo would apply stricter work conditions and would make union supporters stay longer hours.

A Wells Fargo spokesperson said the bank trains its managers to respect the rights of its employees to freely associate and join or support a union, or to bargain collectively with a representative of their choosing.

“We train our managers to comply with labor law and respect the rights of our employees,” the spokesperson told Banking Dive via email. “In this case, the majority of eligible employees freely voted against a union in a Board supervised secret ballot election and the facts do not support allegations to the contrary.”

Wells Fargo is cooperating with the investigation but believes these allegations are unfounded and plans to defend the company and employees, the spokesperson added.

An NLRB hearing before a judge is scheduled for October, and Wells Fargo, if ordered to collectively bargain, can appeal to NLRB members in Washington, Bloomberg reported.

Recently, unionized Wells Fargo employees hit a new challenge in organizing. The bank's conduct management intake team won its union vote 21-16 in December, making it the first non-branch unit at Wells Fargo to unionize.

The team, which handles customer and employee complaints across various locations, has now filed an unfair labor practice charge with the NLRB through Wells Fargo Workers United-CWA. The complaint alleges that the bank illegally refuses to engage in collective bargaining following the certified union vote, American Banker reported. However, the bank contends it’s waiting for the outcome of the NLRB’s review and claims there were procedural flaws in the handling of the vote.

CWA unionized 24 Wells Fargo branches last year, with around 200 employees being organized.

Wells Fargo CEO Charlie Scharf pushed back on employee unionization efforts last April, saying it’s important to “make clear that we continue to believe that our employees are best served by working directly with Wells Fargo and our leadership team.”

#7799. At Large Circuit Nominees?

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

If the blue slip is abolished for district courts, it should be obliterated for circuit courts.

During the first Trump Administration, the blue slip policy was effectively eliminated for circuit court judges. The goal, of course, was to ensure that states with one or more Democratic senators would not be able to block all circuit court nominees. Still, the blue slip policy remained for district court judges through Trump 1.0, the Biden Administration, and Trump 2.0. Does anyone expect the blue slip policy for district court judges to survive if a Democrat wins the White House in 2028 with 56+ Senators? I am doubtful. Indeed, given how Democrats blocked so many U.S. Attorney nominees, I am doubtful the blue slip endures even for that position.

Let's just assume the blue slip policy is eliminated for district court judges. Should the Republicans ever regain power, I propose a thought experiment: actually eliminate the blue slip for circuit judges. As I've noted, circuit court judges belong to the circuit, not the state. It is a mistake to even think of a "home state senator" for a circuit court seat. Of course seats are affiliated with a state by virtue of custom, but nothing in the statute requires it. If Congress wants to assign a seat to a state, they can easily do so. But a Circuit Court Judge decides cases that affect all of the states in a circuit. Indeed, over time, some seats have "switched" between states.

The President could perhaps facilitate that process by making all circuit court nominees "at large." In other words, the President could solicit nominees from candidates in all states in that circuit. If a Fifth Circuit seat opens up, the Senators from Texas, Louisiana, and Mississippi could all make recommendations, and the President could pick the best candidate all around. Likewise, if an Eighth Circuit seat opens up, the Senators from the states between North Dakota and Arkansas can make recommendations.

First, and foremost, requiring this much consultation can gum up the process. Dealing with one set of senators is a lot of work. Multiplying that by many more can become impossible. But it would be just that--a consultation. The White House would only have to interview the judges that clear the bar. Again, no actual blue slip. I suspect if you rank all of the nominees circuit-wide, few would make the cut.

Second, some senators are very good at picking judges. Opening up the process to so many not-so-good senators, can make the process worse. Indeed, Senators are democratically accountable, while people in OLP and the White House Counsel's Office are largely unknown. I think the response is that very few few Senators are actually good at this process. My goodness, the Senators from Mississippi and Arkansas should be permanently disqualified from picking their friends as judges. I think my recommendation would, on balance, get far more strong judges than the status quo. Of course, the President can give more deference to senators with proven track records of picking judges.

Third, Senators are unlikely to go along with this process, and will not give up their customary prerogative. Again, in my hypothetical, the blue slip is gone for district court judges, so it will be a different world. Indeed, given that district court judges can issue universal vacaturs that affect the entire country, I'm not sure why senators should have that much control. The Senate can of course vote down a nominee, but that would have to be a vote they are accountable for. Would Senators Boozman and Cotton have voted down Judge Rudofsky on the floor? Probably not.

This is just a thought experiment. Fodder to consider for the future. That is, unless the Grand Old Party goes the way of the Federalists and the Whigs.

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7797. Help set the ABA’s new advocacy agenda in D.C.: Take the Legislative Priorities Survey

The ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey. (Al Drago/Bloomberg)

The historic November midterm elections have rewritten the political landscape in Washington, D.C., setting the stage for Democratic control of both chambers of Congress and a potentially consequential legislative agenda.

The 120th Congress convenes in early January to confront the challenges of governing in a divided government. It is important that the American Bar Association is ready to engage and to have a strong voice at the table on issues affecting the legal profession and the administration of justice. As a new balance of political power takes shape during President Donald Trump’s final two years in office, the ABA is inviting all members to help set its advocacy priorities for the 120th Congress through the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey.

Participation in the survey is available exclusively to ABA members. By participating in the survey, you have the opportunity to have your voice heard on issues that matter most to the legal profession and the justice system.

The survey opened Nov. 6 and will close on Dec. 4. Most ABA members have received an email with a personalized link to the survey. But any member can access the survey at ambar.org/priorities. Members can also expect an invitation from ABA President Barbara Howard, and the link will be distributed via the ABA’s social media. With a new political landscape taking shape in Washington, the ABA Legislative Priorities Survey will play an important role in ensuring that the association’s advocacy efforts reflect the concerns and priorities of our members.

The 2026 survey has an even more streamlined ranking system than the last priorities survey. Members are being asked first to prioritize issues aligned with the ABA’s current priorities and policies. Members then respond to open-ended questions designed to identify additional policy issues the ABA should consider prioritizing, including those that might require the development of new policies.

The survey takes less than 10 minutes to complete, and your input will be indispensable to informing the ABA’s legislative priority-setting process.

The survey results will be presented to the Board of Governors at the ABA Midyear Meeting in early 2027. The Board will consider ABA member input, along with the following criteria, to determine whether an issue should be made a priority:

• Breadth and strength of the ABA interest • Importance to the practice of law • Public perception of the profession • Opportunity for impact • Potential for achievement • Timeliness of issue • Expertise of lawyers on the issue • Importance to society • Importance to the administration of justice

The 120th Congress presents new opportunities for the ABA to advance policies important to our members and our legal profession and to work with policymakers as they contend with issues that could have far-reaching consequences for our nation.

Please take a few minutes to complete the survey now. Your input will help strengthen the ABA’s voice in Washington, ensuring that the legal profession’s priorities are heard and its commitment to the rule of law amid the new political realities in Washington, D.C., remain a powerful force in our nation’s capital.

This report is written by the ABA Governmental Affairs Office and discusses advocacy efforts by the ABA relating to issues being addressed by Congress and the executive branch of the U.S. government. Follow @ABAGrassroots on social media.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7795. The SEC has requested to delay climate rule arguments. What’s next?

Sustainable investing experts are not surprised by the delay and say it is expected to have minimal immediate impact.

Acting Securities and Exchange Commission Chair Mark Uyeda’s decision last week to ask the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals to delay arguments for the agency’s climate risk disclosure rule did not come as a surprise to regulatory experts in the space.

While the change is expected to have minimal immediate impact, it sets the stage for a shift in focus for the SEC under the Trump administration.

The SEC issued its long-awaited climate-risk disclosure rule last March, nearly two years after it was first proposed — and amid over 24,000 public comments. Uyeda was one of two commissioners to vote against the rule’s approval. The rule was immediately met with multiple lawsuits that were later consolidated into the Eighth Circuit. The spate of legal challenges led the agency to stay the rule’s implementation in April.

Given the agency’s stay and the change in administration, Tom Willman, regulatory lead for artificial intelligence sustainability platform Clarity AI, said Uyeda’s decision came “as no great surprise.”

“It is nevertheless disappointing that investors will be deprived of much-needed financially material information related to climate related risks,” Willman said by email Wednesday.

Julie Gorte, senior vice president of sustainable investing at Impax Asset Management was more blunt in an interview: “The only person on the planet who didn't see this coming was Rip Van Winkle,” she said Wednesday.

Uyeda’s recommended pullback on defending the SEC climate rule follows his prior critiques of the rule. During the hearing on the final climate rule, in the weeks after it was finalized and in his Feb. 11 statement announcing the delay request, Uyeda maintained his belief that the SEC does not have the authority to promulgate the rule or require such disclosures.

Jenner & Block Partner Jennifer Lee, a former assistant director of the SEC Enforcement Division, said Uyeda’s position is “consistent with the new, Republican-led SEC’s shift back to focusing on ‘bread and butter’ investor disclosure issues.” Lee, who now represents companies and financial institutions in regulatory investigations and litigation, told ESG Dive in emailed comments Thursday that she expects that focus to include an emphasis on materiality, while looking to avoid “overly prescriptive disclosure requirements for public companies.”

The change in SEC posture, however, is expected to have a minimal impact for companies or investors, according to Willman and Gorte.

“The impact of this is going to be extraordinarily minimal, partly because it was never enforced in the first place,” Gorte said Wednesday. “So we never had better climate reporting stimulated by U.S. regulatory postures to begin with. And for U.S. companies, or for any company really, a lot of the big ones are probably still going to have to be reporting on all the same things that were in that rule because of [other jurisdictions].”

Willman echoed that note and said that many U.S. companies already voluntarily report climate risks due to investor demand, in addition to growing regulatory requirements both overseas in jurisdictions like the European Union, and stateside in California. New York recently reintroduced its own version of California’s climate disclosure laws.

Additionally, Stephen O’Day, a partner at Smith, Gambrell & Russell, noted the intervenors in the case could continue the rule’s defense, even though the SEC’s announcement indicates this iteration of the agency is not inclined to defend the rules. In the case of the climate rule, 18 states and the District of Columbia have signed on as intervenors to support the agency’s rule.

O’Day said a similar process happened after intervenors continued the defense for enforcement actions taken by the Clinton-era administration for violations of the Clean Air Act by coal-fired plants. Ultimately, the intervenors prevailed, and the Supreme Court upheld the actions.

“The proceedings pending in the Eighth Circuit involve challenges filed by multiple parties and intervenors, any of which could seek to continue defense of the SEC rules,” O’Day said. “So, while the court may grant the requested 45-day pause, it remains to be seen whether any such pause will result in the end of the SEC’s final rules.”

Regardless, sustainability programs and disclosures are expected to continue.

“Regulatory shifts don’t change the fundamental reality: physical climate risk is already priced into markets,” Lukky Ahmed, CEO of climate risk data and analytics platform Climate X, said by email Wednesday. Firms have a fiduciary responsibility to continue to assess, manage and disclose climate risks to their operations, Ahmed said.

“Integrating climate resilience and adaptation strategies isn’t just prudent — it’s essential for maintaining business performance, driving shareholder returns, and protecting communities," Ahmed said.

Despite the shifting federal policy stance, “there is a lot of faith that the drivers of sustainability remain in place no matter who is in anyone's White House,” Gorte told ESG Dive.

“If we don't solve the climate crisis, there are going to be … parts of the globe that are probably uninhabitable, or where people can't work outdoors in the summer. If we don't solve the biodiversity crisis, the prospects are even worse.” Gorte said. “So there are things that we have to do in order to preserve what we think of as life as we know it, and those drivers are going to remain in place.”

#7792. National Security Division Announces First “Near Miss” Non-Prosecution Agreement Under the Department-wide Corporate Enforcement Policy

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

The Department of Justice announced today that it has entered into a non-prosecution agreement with Extreme Networks, Inc.  The company agreed to pay criminal penalties totaling $975,721.84 to resolve the Department’s investigation of sanctions and export control offenses.

The Department reached the agreement under its 2026 Corporate Enforcement and Voluntary Self-Disclosure Policy (“the Policy”), which incentivizes companies to voluntarily disclose discovered misconduct, cooperate with Department investigations, and timely and appropriately remediate the wrongdoing.

This agreement with Extreme Networks marks the Department’s first non-prosecution agreement in a “near-miss” case under the Policy, meaning a case that involved full cooperation and appropriate remediation but did not qualify for a declination of prosecution.  While Extreme Networks’ disclosure to the National Security Division (NSD) was not timely because it occurred under imminent threat of disclosure by a news publication, Extreme Networks nonetheless fully cooperated with the Department’s investigation and timely and appropriately remediated the misconduct. As a result, its disclosure qualified as a “Near Miss” Voluntary Self-Disclosure under the Policy.

“This non-prosecution agreement and million-dollar criminal penalty mark the successful resolution of our investigation into the illegal sale of advanced networking equipment and services to a Russian weapons manufacturer, in clear violation of U.S. sanctions and export controls,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “The FBI remains dedicated to keeping sensitive technology out of the hands of the Russian military, and we're grateful to Homeland Security Investigations and the Bureau of Industry and Security for their partnership on this case. Let this announcement serve as a clear warning: if you attempt to arm our adversaries by violating U.S. law, justice will find you.”

“HSI remains committed to investigating companies and individuals who evade U.S. export controls and sanctions to provide goods or services to foreign weapons manufacturers,” said Acting Special Agent in Charge Jeremy Pierczynski of Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) Detroit. “These laws protect our national security and prevent U.S.-origin products and services from supporting adversaries’ military capabilities. HSI will continue working with our law enforcement and regulatory partners to identify and hold accountable those who undermine these critical safeguards.”

The agreement arose out of an investigation into Extreme Networks’ sales of products and services to Moscow Machinery Building Plant Avangard (MMZA), a Russian weapons manufacturer that was owned by JSC Concern Almaz-Antey (Almaz Antey), which was added to the Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List by the Department of the Treasury’s Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in July 2014.

Pursuant to the non-prosecution agreement, Extreme Networks will forfeit $487,860.92 in proceeds from the sanctions and export control offenses and pay a criminal fine of $487,860.92, for a total criminal penalty of $975,721.84. Extreme Networks will also resolve a parallel administrative action by OFAC.

Between around March 2018 and March 2022, Extreme Networks, through its then-Russia based subsidiary, Extreme Networks Rus LLC, processed and fulfilled 11 purchase orders for networking equipment and services to MMZA without the required license or authorization from OFAC. MMZA was a primary producer of the S-300 and S-400 anti-aircraft missile systems used by the Russian army. To facilitate these sales, certain Russia-based Extreme Networks employees concealed the identity of MMZA from Extreme Networks’ global trade compliance group, causing Extreme Networks to file false electronic export information via the Automated Export System and smuggle goods from the United States. Through this scheme, Extreme Networks deprived the U.S. government of its ability to carry out its lawful function of enforcing sanctions and export controls designed to protect national security and economic interests. As a result of its unlawful conduct, Extreme Networks earned approximately $487,860.92 in revenue from the sales of goods and services.

Although Extreme Networks’ self-disclosure to NSD was not timely pursuant to the Policy, Extreme Networks nonetheless cooperated with the Department’s investigation by timely providing relevant facts and documents and making employees available for interviews. Extreme Networks also appropriately remediated the misconduct by terminating its contract with the third-party distributor it used to facilitate these sales, improving screening procedures, hiring additional compliance personnel, and implementing diligence procedures in connection with mergers and acquisitions. Given these steps and the lack of aggravating circumstances, the Department agreed to enter into a non-prosecution agreement.

The FBI Charlotte Field Office, the Department of Commerce’s Bureau of Industry and Security, and Homeland Security Investigations investigated the case.

This case was prosecuted by former Trial Attorney Maria Fedor of the National Security Division’s Counterintelligence and Export Control Section and Assistant U.S. Attorney Adam Hulbig for the Eastern District of North Carolina.

Please see the Justice Department’s policy here.

#7790. Russell Brand sentenced to 10 years following rape and sexual assault conviction

British comedian, actor and podcaster Russell Brand arrives at the Southwark Crown Court in London during his trial on charges of rape, sexual assault and indecent assault. He was convicted and sentenced to more than 10 years in prison. (Photo from Shutterstock)

British comedian and actor Russell Brand was sentenced in London on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison following his conviction for raping one woman and sexually assaulting three others.

High Court of England and Wales Judge Joel Bennathan described Brand, 51, as a sexual predator who used his public standing to shield himself from accountability before women came forward following media reports in 2023, Courthouse News Service reports.

Brand will likely serve two-thirds of his sentence before being released on parole, the judge said. The sentencing followed a four-week trial in which jurors found Brand guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault involving four women between 2004 and 2009. He was acquitted of two other rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.

Before the sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women, who described the lasting effects of the attacks on their confidence, relationships and ability to feel safe.

The judge considered Brand’s charitable work, including helping people struggling with addiction by funding treatment. However, he said good character and exemplary conduct would not normally justify a significant reduction in a prison sentence.

#7788. American Woman Convicted of Receiving Military Training from ISIS in Syria

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Today, a federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Halima Salman, 27, a U.S. citizen and former resident of Brooklyn, also known as “Umm Khattab al-Muhajir,” of receiving military-type training from the Islamic State of Iraq and al-Sham (ISIS), a designated foreign terrorist organization, in Syria. Salman was convicted after a two-week trial before U.S. District Judge Natasha C. Merle.

“The atrocities committed by ISIS, including mass executions, sexual slavery, and the systematic terrorizing of civilian populations, represent some of the gravest crimes of our time,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “There is simply no excuse for aligning with or receiving military training from an organization responsible for such suffering. Today's verdict sends a clear message that those who support this death cult will be found and prosecuted.”

“With today’s verdict, Salman is held accountable for joining forces with a terrorist organization,” said U.S. Attorney Joseph Nocella Jr. for the Eastern District of New York. “ISIS ravaged Syria and caused havoc across the globe; our Office will continue to prosecute those who supported its murderous reign.”

“It’s been nearly a decade since Halima Salman sought military training from ISIS in Syria, and today justice has been served,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI remains unwavering in its vigilance. We will continue to identify, disrupt, and bring to justice those who support foreign terrorist organizations and threaten the safety of our nation and our communities.”

As proven at trial, in September and October 2016, Salman’s parents traveled with her and her eight siblings out of the United States, ultimately destined for ISIS-controlled territory in Syria.

In late 2016 or early 2017, Salman was 18 years old and married to an ISIS fighter in Syria, where she voluntarily sought military-type training and received authorization to carry ammunition and an assault rifle from ISIS. Salman received a document certifying that she successfully completed that training, a copy of which was found on her husband’s cellphone after it was recovered from the battlefield. Also on her husband’s device were photos depicting Salman with an ISIS flag in the background and a video that shows her brandishing an AK-47 rifle.

The case was investigated by the FBI New York Field Office. The Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs provided significant assistance obtaining evidence overseas.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Adam Amir and Amanda Shami for the Eastern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with valuable assistance from Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Reich, Paralegal Specialist Emily Woodruff and Trial Attorney Patrick Cashman of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

#7785. Man Pleads Guilty to Federal Hate Crimes in Deadly Attack on Boulder, Colorado, Gathering

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Mohamed Sabry Soliman, 46, of Colorado Springs, Colorado, pleaded guilty in federal court today to 12 hate crimes charges for using Molotov cocktails to attack members of the group Run for Their Lives and others.

As part of the plea agreement, Soliman admitted that on June 1, 2025, he lit and threw two Molotov cocktails into a gathering of the Boulder chapter of Run for Their Lives, a group that organized walks throughout the United States to raise awareness for hostages still held after the October 7, 2023, terrorist attacks in Israel. Soliman further admitted that he targeted the group because of the victims’ actual or perceived Israeli national origin and Jewish religion. The attack killed one person and caused permanent and life-threatening injuries to several others.

“No one should be subjected to violence because of their religion or national origin,” said Assistant Attorney General Harmeet K. Dhillon of the Justice Department’s Civil Rights Division. “With this plea, we hope to deliver a measure of justice to the victims and their families. The Civil Rights Division remains committed to vigorously prosecuting the perpetrators of bias-motivated violence.”

“By his own admissions, Mohamed Soliman’s hateful attack on our neighbors in Boulder was antisemitic,” said U.S. Attorney for the District of Colorado Peter McNeilly. “All Americans should feel free to pursue their faith and way of life without fear that doing so will put their personal safety at risk. Antisemitism erodes the common ties that bind our great nation together and there is no place for it in America. We are grateful for the trust and support of the victims and the Boulder community as we prosecuted this case.”

“This individual conducted a despicable attack on people he believed to be Jewish or who support Israel, and with today’s plea he is admitting his guilt,” said Assistant Director Jarod Brown of the FBI’s Counterterrorism Division. “The FBI is steadfast in our commitment to protect our communities and uphold the Constitution.  We will continue to work with our Justice Department partners to ensure those who harm others or attempt to intimidate those expressing their personal views are held accountable.”

“The chaos inflicted by this defendant spread its seeds far beyond Pearl Street, Boulder, and Colorado,” said Special Agent in Charge Amanda Koldjeski of the FBI Denver Field Office. “FBI Denver is proud of the role we played in this case alongside our partners in Boulder: We do not tolerate acts of hate and terror against our neighbors. We will continue to work to keep our community safe and seek justice for victims.”

For nine of his hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of life in prison, five years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. For the three other hate crimes charges, Soliman faces a maximum penalty of 50 years in prison to run consecutive to any other prison term, three years of supervised release, and a fine of up to $250,000. A federal district court judge will determine any sentence after considering the U.S. Sentencing Guidelines and other statutory factors. A sentencing hearing is scheduled for Jan. 7, 2027.

The FBI Denver Field Office and the Boulder Police Department investigated the case.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Melissa Basche and Daniel Pastor for the District of Colorado and Trial Attorneys Sarah Howard and Khalil Quinan of the Civil Rights Division’s Criminal Section are prosecuting the case.

#7783. Sheriff allows law firm to profit from policing, lawsuit alleges

Miami-Dade County Sheriff Rosie Cordero-Stutz at a U.S. Senate Special Committee on Aging hearing in Washington, D.C., on April 30, 2025. (Photo by Annabelle Gordon/Sipa USA/Sipa via AP Images)

In a lawsuit that could affect how some forfeitures are handled in Florida, the Miami-Dade County sheriff is being accused of unconstitutionally allowing a law firm to profit when police seize property and cash.

Under federal and state forfeiture law, police departments can seize money or assets, such as boats, that they think were used in crimes or purchased with ill-gotten gains.

Mobile phone distributors and retailers in Miami argue that a firm run by Israel “Izzy” Reyes—a former cop, a former prosecutor and a former judge—is representing the sheriff’s office in civil forfeiture cases and keeping 20% to 35% of the proceeds, plus an additional 5% on appeal.

According to court papers filed in October, the companies said their bank accounts were frozen last year, and more than $45.2 million was seized as as part of civil forfeiture cases handled by the firm.

An additional $2.6 billion has also been targeted for seizure, the companies alleged, according to a story by the Miami Herald.

Rosie Cordero-Stutz is the first elected sheriff in Miami-Dade County since the 1960s.

#7781. DEI attacks are likely to refine and improve programs, experts say

The intense pressure to end diversity initiatives has led companies to scrutinize their policies. Many of the attacks will end up strengthening DEI programs.

The politicians, provocateurs and think tanks that in the past few years have worked to dismantle diversity, equity and inclusion may not appreciate the full consequences of their efforts.

They’ve used a variety of tactics, in the public and private sectors, including White House executive orders; lawsuits or the threat of lawsuits; shareholder proposals; and needling on social media. They’ve notched high-profile wins, most notably the Supreme Court’s ruling against affirmative action and capitulation at several companies, including retailers and brands that have ended or scaled back their DEI programs.

The successful challenges, inevitably, are forcing scrutiny of DEI practices. But they also provide an opportunity to reinforce DEI goals and execution, which David Glasgow, executive director of New York University’s Meltzer Center for Diversity, Inclusion, and Belonging, sees as a silver lining.

Indeed, the victories are hardly universal. Because diversity, equity and inclusion are good for business for a variety of reasons, most companies are not abandoning DEI. So far in 2025, Target, Nike and Costco are among those that have defended at least some aspects of their policies (in Costco’s case, vociferously). As the Heritage Foundation, a major DEI foe, noted in November, most Fortune 500 companies continue to publicly commit to DEI.

“It is a time for companies to refine and strengthen their inclusion efforts in ways that reduce the risk in the short term — because the risk is real, and we know that — and in ways that are sustainable in the long term,” said Adrienne Pulido, vice president of inclusion insights at Kantar. “So it is looking at both ends of the spectrum, in terms of being very clear about what inclusion means to their business.”

DEI is being pilloried as discriminatory and unfair, yet these systems are designed to create a business that is neither. That is, a business where employees have a variety of backgrounds and perspectives (diversity); hiring, promotion and other actions are executed fairly (equity); and the culture is comfortable and inviting to all who work there (inclusion).

“Unpacking what DEI is and what inclusion is, is part of this moment we're in and part of the conversation that companies need to have about their strategies,” Pulido said by video conference. “What does DEI mean to the business itself? What does it mean to the business and to the future business? Because the demographics of the country are changing, and our research shows that inclusion as a concept, as an idea, is very popular among Americans of all backgrounds.”

DEI goals for most companies are more important than ever because the markets for their products and services are more diverse than they were a decade or more ago, according to Effenus Henderson, who has worked in recruiting, staffing and succession planning at companies in the U.S. and abroad since the 1970s.

“This attack is amplified through the use of social media and technology and psychometrics, where emotions get aroused and reinforced,” he said by phone. “But fundamental to all this is that DEI is not about creating systems that are discriminatory, or about quotas, or a focus on one thing at the exclusion of others. I don't think organizations have really done that. What they have been doing is really trying to expand participation because of the growing demographic change that we're seeing.”

The need to develop DEI strategies that fit with and further business strategies dictates the involvement of leadership, according to Henderson. Too often, though, they are left to the human resources department, leaving companies at risk of adopting DEI programming that is ineffective and possibly indefensible.

“The companies that are able to navigate this generally are the ones where leadership has spent the time talking about it,” he said. “It's not just about reacting to the George Floyd situation or to civil rights laws or litigation. It's really, ‘How do we integrate this as a part of the DNA of who we are as an organization?’ If your organization is more performative, then they don't really understand how it helps to shape business strategy and policy.”

DEI should be treated like any other strategic priority, according to Tim Heneveld, country director for Pergolux in North America. With DEI under the spotlight, it’s a good moment to reassess whether hiring, workplace environment, leadership and operational strategies fit with broader aims.

“That means setting measurable goals, using data to track impact, and holding leadership accountable,” Heneveld said by email. “Some organizations are feeling pressure to scale back DEI, but I think doing so would be shortsighted. Instead, companies should refine their DEI strategies, aligning them with long-term business goals rather than reacting to what they are seeing in the media or any other outside factors. I've experienced, firsthand, workplaces can attract top talent, strengthen their teams, and improve retention.”

In some cases, companies are continuing with their DEI efforts, but changing the names of their initiatives or titles of their employees, experts said.

Crafting DEI initiatives and training is always a work in progress because businesses, markets and demographics evolve, according to Henderson. For many companies, that may mean avoiding those three letters of the alphabet, or the words “diversity, equity and inclusion.” But that, too, requires some thought, he said.

“Is continuing to refer to it under those banners still appropriate, and if I look at renaming it, am I doing that to help enhance our appeal to the markets of the customers and employees we serve? Are we doing it as a reactive, defensive thing for a short-term issue that's hot and heavy right now?” he said. “Get clarity around your objectives, the alignment with your strategies, and then decide whether how you are framing it today will work for you tomorrow and the day after. At some companies, it may mean one thing, and to others it may mean something else.”

The list of lawsuits against DEI programs tracked by the Meltzer Center is long, and getting longer.

Most of these claims invoke civil rights laws intended to end or prevent unfair hiring practices or contracts. Frequently that includes Title VII of the Civil Rights Act, barring discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex and national origin; Section 1981 of the federal code barring discrimination in contracts; and the U.S. Constitution’s equal protection clause, according to Glasgow. The Meltzer Center advises companies to avoid DEI practices that give preference to members of certain groups and involve a tangible benefit.

Evaluating whether a company’s DEI programs run afoul of the latest interpretations of these codes entails enlisting attorneys or other compliance experts.

“This has become a thriving legal practice area,” Glasgow said.

Any business strategy should always be grounded in risk mitigation, and this is just another place for companies to check, according to Henderson. Companies may learn that, to avoid risk, certain aspects of their DEI programs should change.

Others may find that they pass muster. In its proxy statement urging shareholders to vote against a proposal that could have weakened its DEI programs, Costco’s board of directors made clear that the retailer regularly evaluates its “practices concerning compliance with law, including evolving Supreme Court decisions.”

In describing how Costco obeys the law and does not discriminate in hiring, promotion and other practices, the board also provided a litany of protected statuses. This is a reminder that, while civil rights statutes are being leveraged to overturn DEI practices, they nevertheless do bar discrimination for a host of reasons. Moreover, any company that does business abroad will encounter antidiscrimination law that isn’t being disrupted by political activism the way it is in the U.S., Henderson said.

“If you look at Canada, Europe, Asia and South America, there are regulations and laws that support and value diversity,” he said. “So backing away from DEI may, in fact, create harm for your business strategies in other parts of the world. It's not a simple answer, and it just depends on who you are.”

While it may seem like DEI programs are quickly getting scrapped in order to avoid controversy, most are simply under review, Glasgow and others said.

“I think it's prompting a much deeper reflection within companies, not just on what is strictly legal or illegal in what we're doing, but on what has been working and what has not been working,” Glasgow said. “Could we be doing this work more effectively, in a way that actually helps us achieve our business goals, or helps us create the kind of culture that we want to create? Are there things that have been low impact, or maybe even have a negative impact, that we should get rid of, even if it's not for legal reasons? I think the moment that we're living in now could be a helpful reset moment for the field.”

#7780. Carter Wilson on justice, manipulation, and why revenge thrillers are so satisfying

I love a revenge thriller! Someone gets horribly wronged, the people who are supposed to help prove useless, and eventually the wronged person decides, screw it, I’ll handle this myself. Things often get bloody from there. Count me in.

We all love justice served when the systems supposed to deliver it have failed. How many of us have felt purely homicidal after getting lost in an insurance company’s endless phone menu? You’ve entered your policy number four times, explained your problem to three people, and been transferred to a department that may or may not exist. Meanwhile, a recording keeps assuring you that your call is important.

Important to whom? Certainly not whoever just disconnected me.

Sure, a bureaucratic phone tree isn’t (usually) justification for a killing spree. But that feeling of powerlessness is familiar. Someone else controls the outcome, and you can’t even get them on the goddamn phone. A revenge thriller transfers power from the system to the individual. The person who’s been ignored or screwed over gets to decide what happens next.

I’ll readily admit there’s emotional manipulation involved. Give readers someone to care about and a good enough reason to want payback, and suddenly they’re willing to entertain all sorts of behavior. This works in David-versus-Goliath stories, too. Show me a corporation knowingly poisoning a town’s drinking water, and I’m probably going to be pretty flexible about what happens to its CEO in chapter thirty. This includes graphic limb removal.

Dexter takes this flexibility to impressive lengths. His code gives us permission to root for a serial killer. We know whom he’s targeting and why, and that’s enough to get us on board. Murder remains bad, of course. We’d just appreciate it if he could finish this particular one before anyone interrupts.

Victoria Helen Stone’s Jane Doe gives us a different kind of payback. Jane makes herself into the perfect girlfriend for a man she intends to destroy. He thinks he understands who she is, while the reader knows how badly he’s miscalculated. There’s something wonderful about watching a man remain so confident while getting everything so wrong. By all means, buddy, keep underestimating her.

But writing about revenge makes me consider what I’d actually do if something terrible happened to me or someone I loved. I get to explore those thoughts while sitting safely in a coffee shop with my laptop. Sometimes I don’t particularly like the answer. Sometimes I love it.

We have laws telling us what’s allowed. We have society telling us what’s acceptable. Then we have our own private understanding of good and evil, which may come with a few footnotes. Don’t hurt people. Don’t kill people. Unless, perhaps, those people are threatening your child.

That last one can do a lot of damage to an otherwise sound moral philosophy.

When I was writing When They Find Me, I never had trouble rooting for Annie Wolfe. She’s hiding with her twelve-year-old daughter, Coral, in a remote Colorado town, all because she took matters into her own hands four years ago and a couple thousand miles away. She knows her vengeance comes with a cost, and she’s waiting to be hunted down. She’s peppered her cabin with hidden weapons and built a safe room.

Then a father and his two adult children invade Annie’s house believing someone else lives there, and a historic blizzard traps everyone inside. This is bad news for Annie and Coral. It’s also an unfortunate development for the people who picked this particular cabin.

Annie will do anything to protect her daughter. I wasn’t sitting at my laptop wishing she’d consider a more measured response while armed strangers threatened them. I wanted her to have easy access to a pickaxe and a flamethrower. But Annie isn’t enjoying any of this. She just wants herself and her daughter to survive. Mostly, she just wants everyone to leave her the hell alone.

Her history with revenge is complicated, and I’ll leave the specifics for readers to discover. Annie believes in an eye for an eye. She has her own sense of proportion, and she isn’t interested in drawing out someone’s suffering. I understood her reasoning even as I wrote about the consequences.

Then there’s Coyote, the father leading the home invasion. He sees himself almost as an animal, acting according to instinct. In his belief system, nature doesn’t concern itself with good and evil. He isn’t waking up, stretching, and wondering how much bad shit he can squeeze in before lunch. He’s doing what comes to him naturally, and I had to take that posture seriously while writing him, even while I wanted Annie cave in his skull.

So there I was, drinking coffee and deciding who deserved to die. Maybe my favorite part of being a thriller writer.

I think revenge stories satisfy the part of us that’s tired of waiting for someone else to fix things. Writing them also makes me question how far I’d go once I stopped waiting. I can believe in the law and still find myself enthusiastically supporting a character who breaks it. Put my own family at risk, and who knows what I’d be willing to justify?

Fortunately, when I finish the book, the rules still apply. I have to behave like a reasonably civilized person. Which I fully intend to do.

Unless my insurance company transfers me one more fucking time.

Carter Wilson is the USA Today and Publishers Weekly bestselling author of eleven standalone psychological thrillers. His stories focus on ordinary people pushed into situations where survival and morality collide, and every decision has consequences. His 2025 novel Tell Me What You Did was a national monthly pick by Barnes & Noble, and his work has been optioned for film and television. He hosts the podcast Making It Up, where he has candid, unscripted conversations with fellow authors about what it actually takes to build a writing life. He also founded Unbound Writer, where he works closely with writers through coaching, immersive retreats, and live workshops. A sought-after speaker and moderator, Carter is known for conversations that feel honest, engaging, and a little unpredictable. He lives in Erie, Colorado and travels frequently to teach, interview, and speak. To learn more, please visit www.carterwilson.com

#7779. Florida Man Sentenced for Stealing Millions of Dollars from Lenders Using Sham Cosmetic Surgery Clinics and Stolen Identities

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Today, A Wellington, Florida, man was sentenced today to 84 months in prison for using sham cosmetic surgery clinics and the stolen identities of more than 100 people to defraud medical lenders of approximately $2.3 million, and for fraudulently seeking COVID-19 disaster relief loans.

“Jacquez Tullis built fake medical clinics using stolen identities, including those of practicing doctors and deceased individuals, and used them to steal millions from lenders,” said Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the Justice Department’s National Fraud Enforcement Division. “When the pandemic hit, Tullis then tried to exploit taxpayer-funded relief meant for struggling small businesses. Today’s sentence makes clear that the Fraud Division will hold accountable those who abuse the public’s trust, whether they steal from private lenders or from the American people.”

“The defendant’s actions represent a serious breach of trust, exploiting the identities of innocent individuals and manipulating financial institutions for personal gain,” said Special Agent in Charge Brett D. Skiles of FBI Miami. “Fraud schemes of this magnitude undermine the integrity of our financial system and inflict real harm on victims whose identities are stolen and misused. The FBI remains committed to protecting the American public, holding accountable those who exploit others for financial gain, and pursuing those who believe they can hide behind elaborate schemes.”

According to court documents and admissions in his plea, from approximately April 2018 through February 2024, Jaquez Tullis, 42, and his co-conspirators created six sham medical clinics that claimed to offer cosmetic surgery and other medical services, but provided no real care.  The conspirators registered the clinics with the Florida Department of State using stolen personal identifying information of practicing doctors and others without their knowledge or consent.  In some cases, they listed those doctors as clinic owners on applications to become approved merchants with six medical lenders.  Those lenders, two FDIC-insured banks and four financial technology companies financed out-of-pocket procedures not covered by insurance.

Once the clinics were approved, the conspirators submitted fraudulent credit card applications to the lenders in the names of more than 100 individuals, seeking approximately $3.1 million.  The applications falsely represented that the funds were for cosmetic surgery and other services the clinics would provide.  In fact, the individuals did not know about or authorize the applications and did not need or want any treatment. According to death records, some had died before the dates they supposedly received care.

Separately, from April through August 2020, Tullis submitted at least nine fraudulent applications on behalf of certain businesses to the U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA) for Economic Injury Disaster Loan (EIDL) loans, a federal stimulus program authorized as part of the Coronavirus Aid, Relief, and Economic Security (CARES) Act.  Tullis obtained funds under EIDL program by submitting false and fraudulent loan applications that collectively sought $696,860 in EIDL funds. The loan applications falsely represented, among other things, the business’ number of employees and revenue.

Tullis pleaded guilty on July 21, 2026, to conspiracy to commit bank fraud and aggravated identity theft.

U.S. District Judge Rodolfo A. Ruiz, II, of the Southern District of Florida sentenced Jacquez Dion Tullis, to 60 months on the bank fraud conspiracy count and a consecutive 24 months on the aggravated identity theft count, for a total of 84 months in prison, to be followed by 5 years of supervised release. Tullis was also ordered to pay $2,309,859.44 in restitution, $200 in special assessment, and forfeiture money judgement of $2,309,859.44

Two co-defendants were previously sentenced:

All three defendants were charged as part of the Justice Department’s 2025 National Health Care Fraud Takedown, announced on June 30, 2025.

Trial Attorney Shana Priore of the Fraud Division’s Public Trust and Financial Integrity Section prosecuted the case. Assistant U.S. Attorney Sandra Demirci of the Southern District of Florida handled asset forfeiture.

On April 7, the Department of Justice announced the creation of the Fraud Division. The Fraud Division is laser-focused on investigating and prosecuting those who commit fraud against the American people. The Department’s work to combat fraud supports President Trump’s Task Force to Eliminate Fraud, a whole-of-government effort chaired by Vice President J.D. Vance to eliminate fraud, waste, and abuse within Federal benefit programs.

#7777. 9 great modern locked-room mysteries and thrillers

Modern thriller authors are finding creative ways to reinterpret the locked-room mystery made popular by Agatha Christie. Why are these types of stories getting a reboot? Is it the intrigue of the seemingly impossible crime? Or the specter of the detective and the murderer trapped together with no way out?

Early examples by Edgar Allan Poe and Arthur Conan Doyle involved an actual locked room, with the detective having to figure out how the murderer got in and out unnoticed. Christie interpreted the trope more loosely, penning stories in which a group of suspects is stuck together in an isolated setting, such as an island or a snowbound train.

Today, some of our most popular thriller authors are paying homage to Christie’s work and adding their own individual spin. With settings that span the globe, all of these novels are built on the nerve-wracking premise that there’s a killer among us, and no one is getting out.

Coworkers from a high-tech startup find themselves battling Mother Nature and each other in this taut psychological thriller. What starts out as a posh corporate retreat at a ski chalet in the French Alps turns into a nightmare when the chalet is hit by an avalanche. As the coworkers are trapped together without outside help, relationships fracture. When one of their group turns up dead, the tension hits new heights and paranoia sets in.

Ware deftly ratchets up the suspense one victim at a time and uses shifting points of view to keep the reader guessing until the final reveal.

All of this town’s 205 residents live in a single building in this haunting thriller set on the Alaskan coast. When body parts wash up on the beach, Anchorage Detective Cara Kennedy is sent to investigate, but a blizzard seals off the town’s only access point, trapping the detective, along with the town’s entire population, together in a building with no means of escape. Cara pursues the case through a labyrinth of dark tunnels, cramped apartments, and shadowy hideaways before the true motive behind the crime comes to light.

Yamashita’s starkly unique setting will linger in the reader’s mind long after the final page.

Like Christie’s Death on the Nile, Rhys’s novel takes place aboard a ship, a setting which contributes to the protagonist’s feelings of isolation and claustrophobia. As the world is on the brink of WWII, Lily Shepherd sets out to leave her past behind and make a new life for herself in Australia. On the voyage, she meets a varied cast of characters, all running from something back in Europe.

When a fellow passenger is murdered, Lily realizes she is not the only one aboard harboring dangerous secrets. Cut off from the outside world and mistrustful of everyone, Lily tries to unravel a tangled web of lies and deceits.

Nalini Singh, There Should Have Been Eight

Known for her stunning New Zealand settings, bestselling author Nalini Singh sets this psychological thriller in New Zealand’s Southern Alps. Seven friends gather at spooky old estate and find themselves sharing an uneasy holiday in which long-buried secrets threaten the group dynamic.

When a snowstorm traps everyone together, the truth begins to emerge about Bea, the eighth member of their friend group who died years ago from an apparent suicide. Sealed off from the outside world, the friends must reckon with questions from the past and shocking revelations that spark vicious reactions.

Agatha Award winner Nevada Barr, best known for her mystery series set in the national parks, creates her own special take on the locked-room trope, setting her story against the backdrop of a terrifying wildfire. After flames tear through Lassen Volcanic National Park in California, park ranger Anna Pigeon emerges from her shelter to find two victims, one of whom was stabbed. As a snowstorm bears down, further cutting off a group of fire survivors from civilization, it’s up to Anna to figure out who among them is a killer.

Leave it to the master of the wilderness thriller to create a riveting “locked-room” mystery inside a 100,000-acre national park.

With a nod to Christie’s Murder on the Orient Express, Sager sets this fast-moving novel on a train bound for Chicago. Seeking justice for the 1942 conspiracy that sent her father to prison and destroyed her family, Anna Matheson brings together a group of people for a carefully orchestrated plot to settle the score.

But her plan is thrown into chaos when one of the passengers turns up murdered and Anna realizes she is not the only one aboard who has a secret vendetta. With her original plan derailed and the body count rising, Anna must figure out who is behind the competing plot before she herself becomes a victim.

When Miriam Macy is invited to participate in a reality show on a private island in the Sea of Cortez, she jumps at the chance to get away from her problems. But as Miriam’s travel companions die one after another, she realizes she’ll be lucky to make it off the island alive.

With the jungle closing in around her, Miriam’s reality show becomes a high-stakes game of survival in which her best weapon is her ingenuity and her ability to read people.

An ancestry-test kit sets off a chain of deadly events leading to one of those signature twist endings that Unger is known for. What starts out as a relaxing retreat at a luxury cabin in the woods turns sinister when it becomes clear that one of the guests has a hidden agenda. As a fierce storm hits the cabin, everyone is cut for from communication and confined together with their volatile secrets.

A lifelong Christie fan, bestselling novelist Lucy Foley pays homage to her British compatriot with her atmospheric thriller set at a hunting lodge in the Scottish Highlands. As a group of friends from Oxford University gathers to ring in the New Year, champagne toasts give way to terror when someone turns up dead. Cut off from help by a blizzard, the friends are trapped with the menacing knowledge that one among them is a killer. With lies, secrets, and decades-old resentments bubbling to the surface, the “friends” don’t know whom to trust.

Foley pays further tribute to Christie with her brand-new locked-room mystery, Murder at the Grand Alpine Hotel. Set at an exclusive resort in the Swiss Alps, it’s the first book in the New Miss Marple Mysteries series, in which Foley reprises Christie’s beloved sleuth, Miss Marple. Fans of Dame Agatha, raise a glass!

Laura Griffin is the New York Times and USA Today bestselling author of more than thirty books. She is a two-time RITA Award winner as well as the recipient of the Daphne du Maurier Award. Laura’s newest thriller, Innocence Road, takes place in a fictional small town in far West Texas.

#7775. Former U.S. Government Contractor Pleads Guilty to Spying for Ethiopia
