Abraham Teklu Lemma, 53, of Maryland, a former information technology contractor at the National Reconnaissance Office, the U.S. Department of State, and the U.S. Department of Justice pleaded guilty today to conspiring to commit espionage on behalf of the government of the Federal Democratic Republic of Ethiopia.

Lemma pleaded guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government and has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months.

“Lemma betrayed the United States to an extraordinary degree,” said Assistant Attorney General for National Security John A. Eisenberg. “He exploited his IT administrator access to remove classified national defense information, including Top Secret information, from a secure facility and transmitted it to Ethiopian government officials hoping they would use it to target and kill paramilitary fighters in a regional conflict. Clearance holders pledge undivided loyalty to the United States and bear a legal and moral responsibility to protect classified information. Those who betray this trust will be prosecuted to the fullest extent of the law.”

“For more than two years, Lemma exploited a position of trust to provide highly classified U.S. government information to a foreign government,” said U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro for the District of Columbia. “In doing so, he betrayed his oath, his colleagues, and his country, while jeopardizing our national security. His guilty plea sends a clear message: those who compromise America’s most sensitive secrets will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable.”

“Despite swearing an oath to defend the Constitution of the United States, Abraham Lemma betrayed our country by committing espionage on behalf of the Ethiopian government,” said Assistant Director Roman Rozhavsky of the FBI’s Counterintelligence and Espionage Division. “By his own admission, Lemma provided classified national defense information to Ethiopian officials, who then used it in military operations during an ongoing conflict. This guilty plea should serve notice that the FBI and our partners will work tirelessly to stop foreign intelligence services, and anyone who decides to work with them, against the interests of the United States.”

“Today’s guilty plea makes clear that any attempt to betray the United States, violate the trust of the American people, and compromise our national security will not be tolerated,” said Assistant Director in Charge Darren B. Cox of the FBI Washington Field Office. “Lemma abused his position of trust and access to some of our nation’s most highly classified information, conspiring with foreign government officials to unlawfully disclose materials protected to the highest level. In doing so, he not only endangered our national security but also betrayed the trust placed in him by the American people.”

According to court documents, Lemma held a Top Secret U.S. security clearance. From 2021 until his arrest in August 2023, Lemma conspired with senior Ethiopian government officials to collect and transmit dozens of highly classified documents, notes, materials, and photographs, classified up to the Top Secret/Sensitive Compartmented Information (TS/SCI) level, to Ethiopian government officials. Material identified as “Top Secret” means that unauthorized disclosure of the material is reasonably to cause “exceptionally grave damage to the national security” of the United States.

Much of the highly classified information Lemma shared with the Ethiopian government concerned an armed conflict in Ethiopia. Lemma’s conspirators included senior officials within political, military, and intelligence branches of the Ethiopian government.

During his espionage activities, Lemma took numerous steps to conceal his conduct. and surreptitiously removed classified documents and information from U.S. government holdings.

Specifically, Lemma wrote notes by hand with classified information and then hand-carried those notes out of secure U.S. government facilities. Additionally, as an IT administrator, Lemma removed electronic versions of classified information from classified U.S. government repositories and then removed the same classified information from secure U.S. government facilities where he worked.

On some occasions, Lemma encouraged his Ethiopian government conspirators to take direct action against paramilitary groups who were fighting the government of Ethiopia. For example, on Dec. 18, 2021, Lemma told one conspirator, “We have to finish these people once and for all, otherwise there will never be peace in Ethiopia.” Later that day, Lemma shared additional information with his conspirator and wrote, “Please send Dro[nes].”

According to the plea agreement, Lemma agreed to plead guilty to conspiracy to transmit national defense information to a foreign government. If accepted by the court, Lemma has agreed to be incarcerated for a period of between 120 and 262 months. Sentencing is set for April 14, 2027.

The FBI Washington Field Office investigated the case, with assistance from the U.S. Department of State's Diplomatic Security Service.

The matter is being prosecuted by Assistant U.S. Attorneys Tejpal Chawla and Adam P. Barry for the District of Columbia, and Trial Attorney Kathryn DeMarco of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division.

#7774. Jacob Elordi will star in an adaptation of The Executioner’s Song

Fresh off his Oscar-nominated turn as the Creature in Frankenstein, Jacob Elordi is set to star in and produce an adaptation of Norman Mailer’s Pulitzer prize-winning 1979 novel The Executioner’s Song.

The Executioner’s Song is a complex, fictionalizd biography-of-sorts of American murderer Gary Gilmore, who, after being convicted of murdering two men in Utah, insisted on his death penalty sentence being carried out, despite the national moratorium on capital punishment implemented by the Supreme Court case Furman v. Georgia, which decided that different states’ inconsistent approaches toward criminal execution violated the Eight and Fourteenth amendments. Gilmore, who fought anti-capital punishment attorneys insistent on preserving his life, was eventually executed by firing squad in 1977.

The novel is broken up into two sections: “Western Voices,” and “Eastern Voices.” The first part is about the forces that made Gilmore into the man he became (including a youth spent in child detention facilities in the barren American west), while the second is about the media frenzy and national debate around the case, and spotlights, in particular, Gilmore’s relationship with the celebrity photographer Lawrence “Larry” Schiller, who conducted many interviews with Gilmore, his family, and others related to the case and brought the project to Mailer, in the first place.

Mailer continued Schiller’s research to craft a nearly 1000-page, plainly-written epic about the nihilism of the American West, the American proclivity towards violence, media madness, the exploitation of the working class, and the cult of white male loneliness. In her review in The New York Times Book Review, Joan Didion raved about Mailer’s accomplishment, calling it “an absolutely astonishing book,” and noting how it shocked her by being about something much more than what it initially seemed: “The Executioner’s Song did not suggest, in its inception, the book it became,” she wrote. “It began as a project put together by Lawrence Schiller, the photographer and producer who several years before had contracted with Mailer to write “Marilyn,” and it was widely referred to as ‘the Gary Gilmore book.’

It seemed one of those lives in which the narrative would yield no further meaning… What Mailer could make of this apparently intractable material was unclear. It might well have been only another test hole in a field he had drilled before, a few further reflections on murder as an existential act, an appropriation for himself of the book he invented for An American Dream, Stephen Rojack’s The Psychology of the Hangman. Instead Mailer wrote a novel, a thousand-page novel in a meticulously limited vocabulary and a voice as flat as the horizon, a novel which takes for its incident and characters real events in the lives of real people.

What she found instead, she writes, was a novel telling a story of a uniquely American desperation. She marvels at how Mailer uses his sentences to convey this above all else: the countless failed attempts for relatedness between people and things, with the sparseness of his prose summoning a “search for a field of negative energy linking these events and these people and the empty melancholy of the place itself.”

She also notes, with surprise, that the strongest of the novel’s voices are the women: “Men tend to shoot, get shot, push off, move on. Women pass down stories.”

Schiller and Mailer had collaborated as photographer-and-writer on numerous projects, beginning with 1972’s Marilyn: a Biography, and The Executioner’s Song is unquestionably their most monumental. Schiller, who directed the 1982 film adaptation of the novel starring Tommy Lee Jones, will executive-produce the new adaptation.

Elordi, who rose to stardom in HBO’s Euphoria, will play Gilmore (a fortuitous thing, given the resemblance between the two men). Elordi has been gravitating to literary projects—most obviously Frankenstein (for which he was nominated for every major acting award). Recently, he has also starred in Emerald Fennell’s 2026 adaptation of Emily Bronte’s Wuthering Heights, and the miniseries adaptation of Richard Flanagan’s Booker-prize winning novel The Narrow Road to the Deep North which was released on Prime Video, last year. Recently, he also played Elvis Presley in Sofia Coppola’s Priscilla and co-starred in Ridley Scott’s postapocalyptic thriller The Dog Stars.

This marks Elordi’s first turn as a producer (not executive producer); Scott Stuber of United Artists and Nick Nesbitt will produce, in addition to Elordi’s manager Matt Vioral and Sherry Marsh.

Schiller, whose photographic legacy is entwined with the landmark moments of the 20th century, was the last person to photograph Marilyn Monroe before she died. He also photographed Lee Harvey Oswald the night he was killed, and Jack Ruby moments after he killed Oswald. He photographed Paul Newman and Robert Redford on the set of Butch Cassidy and the Sundance Kid (and also directed the photographic section of the film), and captured the Watts riots and the Electric Kool-Aid Acid Tests. He captured landmark touchdowns by O. J. Simpson and Muhammad Ali defeating Floyd Patterson to win the World Heavyweight Boxing Title. As a filmmaker, he made numerous projects for television, and won an Emmy in 1986 for his adaptation of Peter the Great. He collaborated with O.J. Simpson on a book called I Want to Tell You, while Simpson was in prison, and after he was acquitted, collaborated with former Time magazine journalist Jim Willwerth to write the New York Times bestseller American Tragedy: The Uncensored Story of the Simpson Defense. His photos and stories appeared in countless publications, including Life, Paris Match, The New Yorker, Time, Newsweek, and the Saturday Evening Post.

Olivia Rutigliano is an Editor at Lit Hub and CrimeReads. Her other work appears in Vanity Fair, Vulture, Lapham's Quarterly, AirMail, the Los Angeles Review of Books, Public Books, The Baffler, Bright Wall/Dark Room, Politics/Letters, The Toast, Truly Adventurous, and elsewhere. She has a PhD from the departments of English/comparative literature and theatre at Columbia University, where she was the Marion E. Ponsford fellow. She hosts the podcasst "Culture Schlock" at Lit Hub Radio. She is on instagram at @oldebean, twitter at @oldrutigliano, and bluesky at @oliviarutigliano.bsky.social.

#7773. Top Dallas County investigator arrested, charged with wife’s murder

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, the chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office, was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment. (Photo from the Dallas County Sheriff’s Department)

The chief investigator for the Dallas County public defender’s office was arrested and charged with first-degree murder Saturday after his wife was found dead in their apartment.

Jimmy Harold Spurger Jr., 54, who has worked for the public defender’s office for nearly 14 years, was married to his wife, Maria Teresa Spurger, for 35 years but filed for divorce in late October, according to Fox 4.

Local first responders who were conducting a welfare check Friday night forced their way into the apartment, where they found Spurger’s wife unresponsive on a couch with a knife in her neck, Fox 4 reports. Spurger also was found in the apartment, covered in blood and sitting next to a knife in the bedroom.

After responding officers found multiple pill bottles also covered in blood, they suspected that Spurger had ingested pills and transported him to the hospital, Fox 4 reports. He was later taken into custody and is being held on a $1 million bond.

Spurger has led the Investigative Division for the Dallas County public defender’s office for 11 months, Fox 4 reports. Previously, he spent more than 13 years in its Capital Murder Division. He also worked for more than 20 years in law enforcement, which included supervising investigations in the Child Abuse and Family Violence Division of the Dallas County district attorney’s office.

Dallas County Chief Public Defender Christi Dean told Fox 4 that Spurger was “an exemplary colleague,” and that “it’s hard to imagine that he has been charged with murder.”

“We know in our profession that the probable cause affidavit doesn’t tell the whole story,” Dean also reportedly said. “The media reports don’t tell the whole story. And we’re still in preliminary stages.”

#7770. Katie Collom on exploring her relationship with true crime in a suspense novel

My first encounter with the genre was during an annual trip to visit my grandma. Each year, I’d dive into the pile of Reader’s Digest she’d acquired, devouring them cover to cover. It was in one these that I read an article about a criminal profiler who suffered a mental breakdown.

This left a deep impression on my eleven-year-old mind. I couldn’t believe there were human beings who could commit acts so horrific, they actually drove their pursuers insane. More importantly, there were people whose jobs were to figure out how sociopaths think!

I continued to seek out more content about criminals and their crimes. The effect could be…less than healthy. I recall spending a night at a friend’s house and being unable to sleep because it was located somewhat near a railroad track. Just the week before, I’d watched a show about a killer who chose his victims by their proximity to the trains he freight-hopped.

Later as a teenager, my worries became more specific: I’d fret daily about my parents properly locking the windows and doors in our home before we all went to bed. Thankfully we didn’t have a basement or an attic because if we did, I probably wouldn’t have ever gotten a solid night’s sleep.

It wasn’t until I was an adult that these types of articles and shows were given a label. By then, true-crime podcasts and TV series had become so trendy they were their own genre. The sudden abundance of content seemed tailor-made for someone like me: a person who’d been consuming these stories steadily from childhood. Even better, there was a whole community out there, who shared similar obsessions.

(If you’re here, reading this essay, it’s fair to say you know exactly what I mean. You’re one of my people!)

In my new thriller, The Terrarium, my main character is a true-crime obsessed cat sitter named Annie. The isolating nature of her job—going into people’s homes to care for their cats—lends itself to a lot of introspection. For Annie, it manifests in her fanaticism for a podcast called Cuppa Crime.

Her relationship with Cuppa Crime is an emotional crutch. Its hosts, Gail and Gary, Annie’s voices of reason. Whenever she’s anxious, afraid, or bored, she escapes into the tales of heinous crimes that Gail and Gary spin on their podcast. I was interested in seeing how far I could push Annie’s obsession. In turn, this made me stop and study my own relationship with true crime.

Like Annie, I’m a bit of a cliché: a millennial woman who probably consumes just a little too much true crime. It’s no secret that the audience leans very heavily toward women. Additionally, the victims in most popular stories—whether that be books, podcasts, or TV series—also tend to be disproportionately women.

In some ways, this makes it easy to explain away any discomfort I might feel around the genre. I rationalize that I consume it to learn how to protect myself as a woman. Or because I can empathize deeply with the female victims. Or because I want to gain an understanding of how evil people think.

In The Terrarium, Annie drip-feeds herself a constant stream of true crime. Her fascination with it veers into paranoia, and yet, she doesn’t see a problem with it because her overconsumption is for the ‘right’ reasons. Annie’s goal is to unravel the mysteries featured in the Cuppa Crime episodes she listens to. She wants justice and therefore struggles to see when it’s all too much.

Granted, a lot of Annie’s choices are downright chaotic and not things I’d ever do. But I also know how easy it is to cross the line between a healthy amount of true crime and consuming so much that it starts to have a very real effect on your life.

While all my reasons for engaging with the genre ring true, there is a point where too much knowledge becomes a jumble of information with few tangible benefits. Will listening to yet another podcast episode or watching another documentary really teach me how to better protect myself, to empathize, to understand the way the mind of a psychopath works (spoiler: you can’t and never will)?

Since these books, podcasts, and shows are presented as entertainment, it can be easy to consume it the same way you might binge Love is Blind. When the subject matter is so dark, too much too fast can be dicey.

I’m not planning to give up true crime any time soon—like I said, we go way back. But I’m learning to find a balance between prioritizing my mental health and still enjoying a hobby I’ve had since I was a kid.

Real mysteries continue to fascinate me (I am a thriller writer after all) and there’s nothing quite like sinking your teeth into a well-done series. And…if it’s okay to wear shirts with a stranger’s name on them and get way too invested in a bunch of guys throwing a ball around, I think spending your time engaging with true crime is equally valid.

It just doesn’t hurt to be a little more intentional. To pause and consider my reasons for listening to, watching, or reading something in the genre and the impact it can have on me. I remind myself that it’s okay to take a break! These stories will still be there when I’m ready to come back to them.

In some ways, I see myself in the paranoid cat-sitter I’ve created, and I hope you will too. Annie was a fun character to write and, hopefully, a fun character to read in a sort of peek-through-your-fingers way. She certainly has some entertaining ways of coping with her love for true crime, but that’s what makes her so compelling.

Like Annie does with Cuppa Crime, you might just get more than you bargained for when you step into The Terrarium. But don’t worry, you’ll be fine. Just keep your wits about you and (as Gail and Gary like to say) always trust your gut.

Katie Collom is the author of Peter Miles Has to Die. She grew up in Mazatlan, Mexico, and is a life-long expat and world traveler. She spent four years in Texas and has carried a piece of it with her ever since. Currently, she resides in York, England, with her husband and three cats.

#7767. Deep cuts: The vampire stories that inspired Caitlin Starling’s new novel, ‘Milkteeth’

You’ve watched or read (or both!) Interview with the Vampire, Dracula, Sinners, and all the other heavy-hitters, you’ve dabbled in playing Vampire: The Masquerade…now what?

You could always check out Milkteeth, my newest novel, which asks the burning question: what if vampires had to breastfeed?

…I promise it makes more sense in context.

More seriously, it’s about Beatrice, a vampiric broodmother; she raises the fledgling children of other vampires through the first three years of their transformation, until they are both mentally mature and able to consume human blood safely. Beatrice is very good at what she does, but she’s looked down on with a certain amount of disgust by the vampires who rely on her.

When she takes on a challenging new charge and her body begins to change in inexplicable ways, she has to figure out a solution before everything can be taken for her—or worse, she devours her own brood.

It’s equal parts domestic and rancid, filthy and tender, violent and intimate. And if that’s less your speed, or you want to see some of the works that are responsible, at least in part, for Milkteeth’s existence, here are some lesser-known vampire stories that I’ve enjoyed.

If you’ve heard of anything on this list, I’d wager it’s this show. Running three seasons on Showtime, Penny Dreadful brought together a broad variety of Victorian pulp horror into an atmospheric, brutal, and occasionally messy symphony. While there are a lot of moving parts, Eva Green’s character, Vanessa Ives, finds herself embroiled on a take on Dracula that is lushly horrific.

The combination of corrupted filth and glittering set pieces across the span of the series epitomizes one of my favorite things about vampire stories: how the seduction and the rot are one and the same, and are inextricably linked.

Buehlman’s novel, set in the 1970s Manhattan subway system, is horrifically, wonderfully rancid, with an all-consuming voice and style. His vampires are monsters in every sense of the word, and their charisma comes from their monstrosity, not in spite of it. He also poses a question that I loved, and kept in mind when writing Milkteeth: what would scare a vampire?

Tom Hiddleston and Tilda Swinton star as Adam and Eve, two vampires who have loved each other for centuries, but often spend long periods apart. When Adam descends into a deep depression, Eve comes home to visit.

The movie is a meditation on music, art, and, ultimately, faith in the coming and going of cycles, and the ability of even the unchanging undead to reinvent themselves on occasion. It’s also occasionally hilarious. Seeing this in a little independent theater with a glass of red wine indelibly shaped the writer I grew into.

Speaking of formative vampires, I saw Hellsing for the first time shortly after it was translated into English. It’s on the dark and brutal side of vampire stories, filled with vicious killers, relentless cravings for blood, and a large helping of ominous and cruel bureaucracy. Alucard, bound to serve the descendants of Abraham Van Helsing, seeks out and destroys other undead monsters, but he’s hardly tame. It’s a great reminder that vampires hunt; it’s definitional.

Hellsing has more than a few adaptations, including Hellsing Ultimate, which stays closer to the original manga source. I think I owe myself a rewatch!

If you prefer your vampires more on the domestic side, Dead Collections is a brilliant, funny, and intimate take on the genre. Sol, an archivist who also happens to be a vampire, and so rarely leaves his place of work, falls in love with the widow of a television writer come to donate the papers of her late wife, and in the process begins to grapple with what his vampirism really means. Like the archive he works in, he’s now immortal…but always at risk of arbitrary destruction.

And while vampire stories often deal with legacy and the hidden costs of immortality, Dead Collections does it all from a delightfully fresh (and queer) angle. In particular, its focus on coming to terms with a changed body echo through Milkteeth.

I read Woman, Eating while editing Milkteeth. The two are quite different, with Woman, Eating centering on a young vampire trying to engage in the larger mortal world, and her experiences with art and isolation, but they both return again and again to that most central vampiric curse: the endless hunger.

Try Woman, Eating if you’re in the mood for something on the literary side that will still manage to unsettle you.

There’s a wide world of vampire-inspired stories out there. If any of these stories capture you, follow where they lead. You may discover a whole new way to look at our favorite thirsty monstrous mirrors.

Caitlin Starling writes horror-tinged speculative fiction of all flavors. Her first novel, The Luminous Dead, won the LOHF Best Debut Award and was nominated for both the Bram Stoker and Locus Awards. She is also the author of the gothic horror tales Yellow Jessamine and The Death of Jane Lawrence, as well as a novella in the Vampire: The Masquerade audio collection, Walk Among Us. Her nonfiction has appeared in Nightmare and Uncanny. Starling also works in narrative design, and has been paid to invent body parts. She's always on the lookout for new ways to inflict insomnia.

#7765. Judge halts CFPB firings

In the same order, the bureau was told not to delete any agency data or transfer its reserve funding to the Fed or anywhere else. The CFPB then reportedly placed most workers on administrative leave.

A federal judge has ordered the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau and its acting director, Russ Vought, not to terminate any agency employee except for cause related to job performance or conduct until March 3, when another hearing in the case will take place.

The bureau responded, however, by placing on administrative leave all employees except those asked to return to work by “the Acting Director, Chief Legal Officer, or another designee,” according to an email from the CFPB’s human capital operations manager that was seen by Bloomberg Law.

The court order on Friday came after the National Treasury Employees Union urged Judge Amy Berman Jackson on Thursday to block Vought from a “mass firing” it believed would affect 95% of the bureau’s workforce as early as Friday.

In the same Friday order, Berman Jackson demanded that the CFPB “not delete, destroy, remove, or impair” any data or agency records covered by the Federal Records Act.

Berman Jackson also ordered the CFPB and Vought not to transfer money from the bureau's reserve funds, other than "to satisfy” the agency’s “ordinary operating obligations.” That includes returning money from the CFPB’s reserve funds to the Federal Reserve, as Vought said this month he would do.

The data-related developments follow a declaration the CFPB’s former chief technologist, Erie Meyer, filed with the court Friday, warning that databases holding 12 years’ worth of information the agency has collected would soon be deleted and “irretrievably lost.”

Affected data would include “supervisory and examination records of financial institutions, enforcement action data, consumer complaints, personal consumer information, and market research records,” Meyer wrote.

Loss of data that tracks institutions’ financial behavior “would impair the Bureau's ability to identify risks and respond to emerging threats within the financial system,” Meyer wrote.

“This could destabilize markets, allow bad actors to exploit weaknesses in financial institutions, and undermine public trust in the financial system,” she wrote.

It would also open the financial system to market manipulation, Meyer asserted.

“Tech companies moving into financial services could gain an illegal competitive advantage by accessing sensitive consumer financial data or enforcement records, and the audit logs of that activity could be deleted,” she wrote. “This could result in unfair competition and undermine market integrity.”

That may serve as a reference to X Money, the payments tool set for launch this year in a partnership between card network Visa and social media platform X, owned by Trump adviser Elon Musk, who’s also seen as the architect behind the Department of Government Efficiency, which infiltrated the CFPB this month.

The deletion of CFPB data “would leave consumers without critical recourse in the event of financial harm caused by institutions under the Bureau's jurisdiction,” Meyer wrote. Further, she asserted, it would make the CFPB’s Consumer Response database “unavailable and/or unreliable, severely hamper — if not entirely take down — the Bureau’s website, and likely result in the loss of mandatory public reporting the Bureau has previously done.”

Friday’s order may represent a relief to CFPB employees, but it doesn’t apply to bureau employees who have already been terminated. The agency last Tuesday terminated roughly 70 probationary employees, then Thursday fired another 70 to 100 term employees – those whose contracts have set limits between one and four years.

Altogether, last week’s firings cut roughly 10% of the CFPB's workforce, according to American Banker.

The CFPB was not the only banking regulator to see workforce reductions last week. Roughly 500 employees at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp., or about 8% of its workforce, accepted a deferred resignation offer from the Trump administration, Bloomberg Law reported Friday, citing a spokesperson for the agency.

The FDIC then terminated probationary employees, the outlet reported Monday, though the number of employees affected remained unclear.

An FDIC spokesperson on Friday did not detail how deeply certain units of the regulator were affected.

A lawyer representing the CFPB workers’ union laid out the urgency of Friday’s court action.

”I’m asking that they don't fire the entire agency tonight,” Deepak Gupta, a founding principal at Gupta Wessler, told the court, according to American Banker. “I don’t want to leave the courthouse without some assurance that the mass layoff is not going to happen and then become a fait accompli.”

The workers’ union asked Thursday for a temporary restraining order to stop the firings, but agreed to seek a preliminary injunction instead.

That mirrors a case in the U.S. District Court for the District of Maryland, in which the city of Baltimore sued the CFPB, claiming Vought’s move to return the agency’s funding to the Fed would effectively shut down the bureau “by fiat.”

The government agreed Thursday that Vought would refrain from transferring money out of the CFPB’s reserve fund or returning money to the Fed or Treasury until Feb. 28, or upon a “contrary order” from the court, Bloomberg Law reported.

Still, in the workers’ union case, Brad Rosenberg, a Justice Department special counsel, objected to the request for a preliminary injunction.

"We don't think any preliminary relief is appropriate at this stage because we don't think the plaintiffs are likely to succeed on the merits," he said, according to American Banker.

Among the employees the CFPB terminated Thursday is Julia Barnard, who served as the agency’s student loan ombudsman since last February. Her position is mandated by the 2010 Dodd-Frank Act.

“This work matters,” Barnard said in a statement issued by the Student Borrower Protection Center. “It’s a lifeline for borrowers and a safeguard against a system that too often fails them. Dismantling this function is unconscionable and will cost real people real money.”

Delaying any further moves to slash the CFPB workforce would at least give employees time to plan and budget for their personal futures. Employees of the agency are entitled by law to 60 days’ notice of job loss. But last week’s firings came with no notice and with immediate effect.

Further, terminations for cause (probationary employees, for example, were notified that they were deemed “not fit for continued employment because [their] ability, knowledge and skills do not fit the Agency’s current needs”) left those employees without access to severance, one lawyer with the CFPB told ABC News.

In Vought’s first week as the CFPB’s acting director, the bureau’s headquarters were closed to employees, who were ordered to stop all bureau work. A tip line was also set up for people to report on employees who might be conducting work.

#7764. Lindsay Clancy loses bid to dismiss murder case with retrial possibility

Lindsay Clancy was being tried for first-degree murder. She admitted to killing her three children and claimed that she suffered from postpartum psychosis. (Photo by CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via the Associated Press)

Lindsay Clancy, a former labor and delivery nurse charged with strangling and killing her three small children in 2023, lost her bid to have her case dismissed Monday, setting the stage for a possible retrial.

Massachusetts Superior Court Judge William Sullivan’s 17-page ruling found that a retrial would not be considered double jeopardy because Clancy’s initial jury was deadlocked.

Clancy, 36, was on trial earlier this year for the strangling deaths of her three young children. The case ended in a mistrial after one juror, known as “Juror Doe,” held out for a conviction. Clancy pleaded not guilty by reason of insanity, alleging that she was going through postpartum psychosis at the time of the tragedy, according to coverage on Courthouse News Service.

Last week, a hearing seeking dismissal of the case explored the role of Michael Desronvil, who is referred to as “Juror Doe” in court records. Desronvil was accused of not following the court’s instructions.

Sullivan found that the evidence “did not reasonably suggest Juror Doe’s inability to deliberate or refusal to follow the law.”

On Nov. 2, the prosecution said it intends to try Clancy again. She initially faced three counts of murder for the deaths of Cora, 5; Dawson, 3; and Callan, 8 months.

#7763. Snowbound suspense: 5 thrillers set during snowstorms

A glorious snowfall can conjure up warm thoughts of hot cocoa, kids tossing snowballs and building forts, the holidays, a still, peaceful white landscape. But it can also create a darker, dangerous flipside. Getting trapped, losing power, being exposed to the elements. I’ve always loved thrillers that take advantage of a bad snowstorm–of bringing cold, heartless motivations to frozen landscapes.

In my latest novel, The Cold Read, I take full advantage of the chilling nature of a snowy locale by setting my book at a remote, abandoned ski resort, where the elements quickly take on a very sinister nature.

Here are a few other books that do the same. If you want to shiver your way through a good mystery without actually having to worry about frostbite, you’ll want to pick up these other snowbound stories as we head into the winter season.

This novel, involving a group of co-workers setting off on a retreat, would be a nightmare on its own even without the thriller elements. Traveling with coworkers! Skits! Presentations! The terror! To make things much, much worse, however, this work retreat involves an avalanche, power loss, and the little matter of the group disappearing and dying off.

The characters make this book the tense, twisty thriller it is. It’s an enjoyable puzzle to piece together as you read.

A group of competitive snowboarding friends reunite in the French alps at the ski resort where their frenemy mysteriously disappeared some years before. But weird things immediately start to happen. Their cell phones disappear and they are cut off from the rest of the world when the  cable cars stop working, leaving them stranded on a dangerous mountain. Tensions abound as past secrets and suspicions start to emerge.

Told in dual timelines, the book does a great job of showing how fierce friendships can be both invigorating and toxic.

Martin Edwards, Miss Winter in the Library With a Knife

Six writers and editors are invited to an exclusive Christmas retreat to play a murder mystery game. The setting is remote, the weather is bad, and the guests all have had recent terrible luck in their careers and relationships.

In a classic Golden Age style with an homage to Clue, the novel sets the reader as another player in the game, complete with a “clue finder” guide and puzzles to solve. When the game becomes reality and people start getting bumped off, all bets are off and the competitive guests have to start playing as though their lives depended on it–because they do.

When a woman and her son arrive on a bus during a snowstorm in New York, escaping an abusive situation, service worker Mattie breaks the rules of her job and brings them to her own house instead of the local shelter. This mistake proves costly as the storm intensifies, an intruder begins to stalk them, and strange things begin happening.

Tightly plotted and claustrophobic, I had a tough time reading this one late into the evening.

The Winter Over follows a small group of Antarctic research scientists setting up for the winter over at Shackleton South Pole Research Facility in Antarctica. They are supposed to be tested physically and psychologically to prepare for the conditions and the loneliness–nine weeks of complete isolation, constant darkness, and extreme cold.

As Cass, a newbie to the job, starts to settle in to her work, a suspicious death of one of the crew makes her wonder if someone on the team might’ve snapped. Trapped at base with a killer and nowhere to go, the team doesn’t know who to trust. What will kill them first? The extreme conditions or the humans on base?

Tara Laskowski is the award-winning author of the suspense novels The Cold Read, The Weekend Retreat, The Mother Next Door, and One Night Gone. She also wrote two short story collections, Modern Manners for Your Inner Demons and Bystanders. She has won the Agatha Award and Thriller Award for her short fiction and was the longtime editor of the online flash fiction journal SmokeLong Quarterly. She lives in Virginia with her husband, crime writer Art Taylor, and their son Dashiell.

#7762. Three Iranian-Backed Operatives Indicted for Their Roles in Nearly 20 Terrorist Attacks and Attempted Attacks Across Europe and the United States

An official website of the United States government

Official websites use .gov A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

Secure .gov websites use HTTPS A lock ( Lock Locked padlock ) or https:// means you’ve safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Note, the release has been updated to include a quote from the National Security Division.

An eight-count superseding indictment was unsealed today charging Mohammad Baqer Saad Dawood al-Saadi, a dual Iranian-Iraqi national; Mohsen Mohajeri, an Iranian national; and Mohammad Ali al-Hassani, an Iraqi national, with terrorism-related offenses for their activities in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations (FTOs), including their involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States, and a September 2026 terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base in Fairford, United Kingdom, where American armed forces were stationed.

“Anyone who plans a terrorist plot on a military base housing American servicemembers will be prosecuted by the United States government,” said Attorney General Todd Blanche. “The defendants listed in the indictment allegedly supported two foreign terrorist organizations, and al-Saadi allegedly coordinated with his co-defendants in the days leading up to the attempted terrorist plot. This Department of Justice will continue dismantling terrorist networks and protecting the American people from terrorist organizations.”

“This eight-count indictment shows the determination of Iran to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the U.S., including one plot that was recently prevented at RAF Fairfield, a British Royal Air Force Base where American forces were stationed,” said FBI Director Kash Patel. “According to the indictment, one of the subjects is behind bars awaiting trial yet he allegedly sent coded messages to assist in future acts of violence. To date, the subjects have been allegedly involved in nearly 20 attempted attacks throughout Europe and the United States in support of Kata’ib Hizballah and Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (“IRGC”), two U.S. designated foreign terrorist organizations. This FBI will use all our resources to detect and stop such terrorist attacks as we’ve done the last 21 months – with over 1,300 terrorists disrupted and nearly 7,000 Foreign Terrorist Organization related arrests, up 1,057%. All those who threaten our homeland will get the message – justice will find you.”

“Today marks a major disruption of an alleged global terrorism conspiracy,” said Acting Principal Deputy Assistant Attorney General for National Security M. Scott Proctor. “No matter where they are in the world, the National Security Division of the Department of Justice will pursue those who target American citizens and American interests.  My thanks go out to the prosecutors and law enforcement partners for their work on this case.”

“As alleged, these defendants helped orchestrate a campaign of terror on behalf of terrorist organizations affiliated with Iran that targeted Jewish communities in Europe and the United States, and the British military base, RAF Fairford, housing American service members,” said U.S. Attorney Jamie McDonald for the Southern District of New York. “Even after one of their co-conspirators was arrested and placed in federal custody, the defendants allegedly continued coordinating terrorist activity through coded communications and a network of associates overseas. The threat presented by Iran and Iran-backed terrorist groups to America and our allies is not hypothetical — it is very real. Our Office will not stop working to address and disrupt this threat, and to prosecute those responsible.”

According to the allegations contained in the superseding indictment and other court filings: Al-Saadi, Mohsen Mohajeri, and al-Hassani allegedly conspired to commit terrorist attacks in Europe and the United States on behalf of an Iran-aligned terrorist network, which included the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, both of which are FTOs. Most recently, in approximately September 2026, al-Hassani allegedly orchestrated a terrorist plot at a British Royal Air Force Base (RAF Fairford) in Fairford, United Kingdom (the “RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot”), which at the time of the attempted attack, housed U.S. military aircraft and personnel.

Al-Hassani and Mohajeri, both of whom were in Iran at the time of the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot, allegedly relied on a network of contacts in the United Kingdom. Al-Saadi, who was imprisoned and awaiting trial on pending terrorism charges in the Southern District of New York, attempted to coordinate with al-Hassani and Mohajeri from jail by passing coded messages through third parties.

Al-Saadi, a longtime operative of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, was charged in May for working with and on behalf of the IRGC and Kata’ib Hizballah, as well as other FTOs, for his involvement in planning and promoting approximately 18 terrorist attacks in Europe; and for attempting to bomb a synagogue in New York. The picture below shows al-Saadi in front of an array of machineguns in a conference room with a map of the United States on the wall next to a list of “legitimate targets” (redacted here) identifying former and current U.S. officials.

As alleged, among the individuals with whom al-Saadi worked to facilitate and carry out the European Terrorist Attacks were Mohajeri and al-Hassani. Mohajeri is an Iranian national and operative of the IRGC who coordinated with al-Saadi and al-Hassani to carry out those terrorist attacks with the IRGC’s backing. Al-Hassani, who is originally from Iraq, used his contacts and criminal associates to carry out terrorist attacks in the United Kingdom.

The European Terrorist Attacks were carried out in the name of a purportedly new terrorist group with the pseudonym Harakat Ashab al-Yamin al-Islamiya (HAYI), which is a front for Kata’ib Hizballah and other FTOs. Of the 18 terrorist attacks in the spring of 2026 for which HAYI claimed responsibility in Europe, seven took place in the United Kingdom, the most of any European country. The attacks involved arsons, explosives, and in one instance, a near-fatal stabbing in London of two Jewish men, including a dual U.S.-British citizen.

Al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and Al-Hassani were allegedly personally involved in planning many of the European Terrorist Attacks, and al-Saadi and Mohajeri helped create and publish online propaganda videos of these attacks. For example, on or about April 6, Mohajeri and al-Hassani planned attacks while together in a room in Iraq with a map of London displayed on a computer screen. In a video of that meeting, al-Hassani told Mohajeri, “we need to get focused on London.”  An image of the video is below, with Mohajeri on the right and al-Hassani on the left. HAYI then claimed responsibility for six terrorist attacks that occurred in and around London starting approximately one week later.

On or about April 17, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri allegedly directed an individual to carry out one of the European Terrorist Attacks in real time. Specifically, al-Saadi, al-Hassani, and Mohajeri, along with others, were in a room watching a FaceTime video with the individual who was carrying out the attack, which was projected onto a large screen against the background of the HAYI logo. Al-Hassani directed the perpetrators’ actions, including by instructing the individual on the other end of the call to execute the attack and directing that individual to take a lighter and “light one in your hand,” “light it,” and “throw the fourth one.” Al-Saadi recorded the attack in real time, while Mohajeri recorded al-Hassani and al-Saadi in the room as they directed the attack. A still image from Mohajeri’s recording, showing al-Saadi (circled in red) and al-Hassani (circled in green), as they directed and filmed the attack, is below.

The next day, on or about April 18, al-Hassani participated in another video call with an individual carrying out an attack on a synagogue in London, with the HAYI logo projected on the background of al-Hassani’s screen. During the video call, al-Hassani directed the individual to “light it up like a Christmas tree.” The person on the video then lit an improvised explosive device and threw it at a building. An image from the video is shown below.

In March and April — overlapping with the time that al-Saadi was co-located in Iraq with Mohajeri and al-Hassani, planning the European Terrorist Attacks — al-Saadi allegedly attempted to coordinate and carry out terrorist attacks in the United States, including by targeting a synagogue in Manhattan.

On or about May 1, following the European Terrorist Attacks, al-Saadi was arrested abroad and subsequently transferred to the custody of the United States to face prosecution. Al-Saadi has been in federal custody since his arrival in the United States. For approximately four months following al-Saadi’s arrest, there were no additional attacks attributable to al-Saadi, Mohajeri, and al-Hassani.

In August, however, al-Hassani allegedly directed and paid associates in the United Kingdom to conduct preparatory steps and arrange logistics for the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot. On Aug. 22, al-Hassani paid one individual (Individual-1) to perform pre-operational surveillance of RAF Fairford’s perimeter and al-Hassani subsequently received videos of the area surrounding the base. In later communications with al-Hassani, Individual-1 referred to him as “Ali.”

In September, al-Hassani also tasked and paid several individuals to help him prepare for the plot, including by procuring vans and barrels of fuel, researching the purchase of chemical accelerants, including large quantities of potassium chloride, and purchasing metallic objects that could be used as explosive shrapnel. At al-Hassani’s urging, those individuals commissioned custom decals that they affixed to the vans to create the appearance that they were used by a fuel delivery business and a swimming pool supply business.

On Sept. 26, al-Hassani allegedly tasked individuals to drive three vans, some of which were later determined to contain barrels of fuel, to the RAF Fairford base. That day, al-Hassani was in frequent communication with the van drivers, helping to coordinate their movements and directing them where to drive. At least two of the three vans, while en route to the perimeter of RAF Fairford, encountered a security roadblock and were not allowed to proceed on their intended route. Al-Hassani communicated with the drivers and occupants of the vans both before and after encountering the security checkpoint. In the early morning hours of Sept. 27, law enforcement authorities in the United Kingdom recovered three white vans to which the fuel delivery business logos were affixed and arrested the occupants.

While in prison in New York awaiting trial, al-Saadi has had phone calls with his immediate family members located in Iraq. As alleged, al-Saadi used those calls to pass coded messages to Mohajeri and al-Hassani in the days leading up to the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

For example, in June and July, al-Saadi allegedly spoke with his mother and sister about Mohajeri. During those calls, they referred to Mohajeri by various aliases, including “Abbas, Abu Daniel” and “Sayyid Abbas.”  Al-Saadi also told his family members that he owed money to Mohajeri and directed them to pass along messages to Mohajeri about “work,” a term al-Saadi regularly used to describe terrorist activity, including on social media posts and in discussions with Mohajeri about partnering to conduct terrorist attacks. On one of those calls, al-Saadi also asked his sister, “What are they doing about all our old work?” and asked her whether it had been cancelled or just put on pause. Al-Saadi’s sister responded that “it isn’t cancelled.”

On or about Sept. 24, al-Saadi once again spoke with his immediate family by phone. On the call, al-Saadi allegedly inquired about how al-Hassani, whom al-Saadi referred to as “Ali,” was doing. Al-Saadi’s family informed al-Saadi that “Ali” had been transferred to the “International Section.”  Al-Saadi then allegedly instructed his family to “give him [al-Hassani] money so we can do it.”  As described above, three days later, al-Hassani orchestrated the RAF Fairford Terrorist Plot.

Al-Saadi, 32, is a citizen of Iraq and Iran. Mohajeri, 48, is a citizen of Iran. Al-Hassani, 35, is a citizen of Iraq. A chart containing the names, charges, and minimum and maximum penalties for the defendants is set forth below.

The Justice Department praised the outstanding investigative work of the FBI’s New York Joint Terrorism Task Force, which consists of investigators and analysts from the FBI, the NYPD, and over 50 other federal, state, and local agencies, and the FBI Washington Field Office, Counterterrorism Division, as well as the assistance of the Department of Justice’s National Security Division, Counterterrorism Section, the Justice Department’s Office of International Affairs, U.S. Customs and Border Protection, the NYPD, the New York State Police, and the Department of State.

Assistant U.S. Attorneys Jeffrey W. Coyle, Sarah L. Kushner, David J. Robles, and Chelsea L. Scism for the Southern District of New York are prosecuting the case, with assistance from James Donnelly and Paul Casey of the National Security Division’s Counterterrorism Section.

A superseding indictment is merely an allegation. All defendants are presumed innocent until proven guilty beyond a reasonable doubt in a court of law.

#7759. The Giggler: The forgotten serial killer who haunted Boston’s South Station

Boston’s South Station was less than 70 years old in 1969 but seemed much older. It certainly lacked the glamour of nearby North Station, home to the Boston Garden, where the city’s basketball and hockey teams played and where the Rolling Stones and James Brown performed for screaming teenagers. In comparison, the South Station stop on 700 Atlantic Avenue was a dreary place for tired daily commuters on their way to the suburbs of the South Shore. With its high-domed ceiling and rickety escalators built during the Depression era, South Station managed to be both enormous and decrepit, a sickly old giant in need of urgent care. As the Boston Globe said a few years later, the once thriving railroad stop was “now staggering along in the last stages of neglect.”

Yet even as it faced the threat of the wrecking ball, the station remained busy, particularly at holiday time. On Friday, December 26, a 9-year-old Dorchester boy named Kenny Martin wandered into the station with a friend, Thomas Lydon. It was the day after Christmas and Kenny, who had come into Downtown Boston to buy some Boy Scout equipment, spent the afternoon horsing around with Lydon at the station. They’d chased each other up and down the escalators, running through the crowd of postholiday shoppers. As the afternoon came to an end, Lydon departed, while Kenny planned to take the train back home.

In his brown-checked jacket with fur collar, blue bell-bottom pants, and orange work boots, Kenny was a typical Dorchester boy, coming home from a day of fun. He was the youngest of four children, small for his age at less than 50 pounds. It might seem odd for a boy so young to be alone in the city, but Boston kids learned to use the subways early in those days. They often traveled on their own from one side of the city to the other.

The platform where he would’ve waited for the Dorchester train was cold and drafty, for there are few places colder than a Boston subway platform in late December. One could only stand and shiver, waiting for the sound of a faraway bell to warn people of approaching trains. Perhaps Kenny looked down the long, dark tunnel for the sign of a subway car’s light, usually visible long before the car was in the station. The tunnels were foreboding; there were stories of people accidentally getting electrocuted on the infamous “third rail” and of huge rodents living in the underground network. Meanwhile, pigeons, bats, and owls roosted in the rafters, occasionally swooping down to frighten the commuters.

There was no shortage of urban legends around South Station, of how people committed suicide by jumping in front of moving trains and how homeless men wandered in the dark tunnels to sleep underneath cardboard coverings. In time, stories of vagrants evolved into stories of trolls living in the tunnels, trolls who only came out after midnight when the station was closed. This was fantasy stuff, tales told by older kids to tease younger ones.

Of course, the station had its good points. It was a historical landmark, after all, opening for business in 1899 as the largest station in the country, a majestic building made of pink granite. There was also the railroad chapel, Our Lady of the Railways. Built in the 1950s, it was the first of its kind in America. Organ music played during every Sunday service, and Boston’s Archbishop Cushing held special masses and Easter vigils, perfect for travelers who couldn’t get home in time to worship. There was a lunch counter, a newsstand, the Sidecar Bar-Grill, a bakery, and a barbershop. A Paramount film crew had been to South Station earlier in the year to shoot a scene for a Jack Lemmon movie, The Out of Towners. For a few days, the dilapidated old station was enlivened by the buzz of Hollywood energy and curious crowds. Despite these occasional bright spots, the atmosphere remained glum and ramshackle. When the crowds thinned out after the rush hour, all that remained were boarded-up areas that always seemed to be “under construction” and weary cleaning crews wiping out the messes of the day.

At some point in the afternoon of December 26, Kenny met a pudgy, dark-haired man with a round face. The man seemed different from the other people hurrying around the station. He was rumpled. He needed a shave and a bath. It turned out the man was also named Kenneth. What they talked about, or how they spent their next few hours together, is unknown. History would reveal that the unshaven man knew all about the secret tunnels in South Station and knew all the special places where people could hide. He may have offered to show Kenny around the old building, an irresistible prospect for a 9-year-old boy.

Kenny’s body was found eleven days later. He’d been strangled to death. His body was hidden in one of the station’s underground passageways. Someone had wrapped it in a canvas bag and covered it with debris. A search team consisting of police from two districts, as well as city engineers, had spent the day exploring sewers and tunnels around the station. The search ended in an abandoned transit tunnel, a ghostly location that had once been used to transport cargo to the surface cars. It was a dingy place for a little boy to wind up, cold and dark and airless.

He could’ve been lured there only by one of the station’s trolls.

Security guards patrolled South Station and routinely tossed out vagrants and drunks, shoving them out the door onto Atlantic Avenue. These scenes were unpleasant, but the guards were under orders to keep the winos and grifters out. The raggedy station only looked worse if pitiful old drunks were lounging on the wooden benches. Yet Kenneth Harrison, the pudgy man, had been living in the place for nearly a year, like a hermit hiding in a cave. He didn’t have to compete for a bed at one of the nearby shelters, not when he could hunker down in one of the abandoned offices beneath the station.

The morning after he’d killed Kenny Martin, Harrison slouched out into the daylight, searching for a rooming house where he could find a bed and lie low. The sidewalk was still slippery from the previous night’s rain and sleet. It would have been a nice day to hang out at the station, yet Harrison felt it was time to go. Hanging around was too risky, even if the dead boy was buried deeper than an old bone.

Harrison had grown up in Roxbury’s Mission Hill neighborhood and had dropped out of school after the eighth grade. Now, at 31, he was an unemployed restaurant worker, living a vagabond’s existence and spending what little money he had on alcohol. He’d become one of life’s losers, a degenerate barfly with no future. He was virtually indistinguishable from dozens of others in his situation. The difference was that Harrison murdered children.

Kenny Martin, whose face would soon be featured in local newspapers, was Harrison’s second young victim. Two-and-a-half years earlier, Harrison had killed a 6-year-old girl named Lucy Palmarin. She’d been cashing in an empty tonic bottle at a store. Witnesses saw her climbing into the car of an unknown man. She was found floating among the garbage in South Boston’s Fort Point Channel, a mile from her home. Since the medical examiner found no signs of injury or foul play, Lucy’s death was ruled an accidental drowning. Lucy’s disappearance created a flurry of activity in South Boston. Posters with her picture were distributed throughout the community. Her poor mother waited up nights, clutching a book of old photographs of the missing girl. Three weeks into the search, the Boston police called in the FBI for assistance. They suspected a kidnapping, but the truth was worse.

On April 15, 1967, Harrison was driving a cab, among his many odd jobs. He would later tell a judge that he had dropped off a fare near the D Street housing project where Lucy lived. He saw her walking and offered to give her a ride. Instead of taking her home, he drove to the channel where he tossed her in the city’s notoriously dirty water.

In another version of the confession, Harrison said the little girl asked him for a quarter, which led to him giving her a piggyback ride. Once she was up on his back, he easily pitched her into the water. So he said. His confessions sounded ludicrous. Lucy’s family was Puerto Rican and new to America. The girl didn’t speak English. In between the two child murders, Harrison had killed two adults. There’d been a barroom beef with a fellow named Joseph Breen, an ex-marine and water company employee. Harrison and Breen had been drinking at the Novelty Bar in Boston’s Combat Zone, a dank neighborhood of nudie bars and X-rated theaters.

Later, after an argument over money, Harrison beat Breen to death with a rock.

Inexplicably, Harrison called the police that night, telling them they could find Breen’s body floating in an excavation pit on Kneeland Street near Chinatown. When the police asked who was calling, Harrison felt a laugh coming up his throat, like an eruption.

It was a time when killers were becoming celebrities, with memorable names and trademarks, like the Boston Strangler or the Zodiac in California. Why couldn’t Harrison be “The Giggler?”

Harrison must’ve felt as elusive as the Zodiac, because he’d actually returned to the Novelty a short time later. A couple of Breen’s friends were there and recognized him as the man who had been with Breen the night he was killed. Breen’s friends called the police, but by the time they arrived, Harrison was gone again, no doubt back at the train station, hiding in plain sight.

Then, just a month before killing Kenny Martin, Harrison had murdered an old woman, 75-year-old Clovis Parker of South Boston. As he’d done with the little girl, he left Clovis floating in Fort Point Channel, a mere five-minute walk from Harrison’s South Station hideout. He’d tell investigators that he had met the old woman on a bridge, and she’d asked for help getting across. Without giving a reason, Harrison said that he’d simply kicked Clovis Parker’s cane from under her and then tossed her over the guardrail. The unfortunate woman’s death hadn’t even made it to the newspapers.

A few days after killing Kenny Martin, Harrison called his sister, Eileen. He confessed that he had killed a boy and told her where the body was hidden. On January 6, the day Kenny’s body was found, Harrison boarded a train at South Station and left Boston.

Eileen consulted a lawyer and then called the police. They followed her tip to find the body, and then a quartet of detectives armed with an arrest warrant traced Harrison to Providence. They arrested him without incident and held him without bail in Suffolk County.

While detectives questioned him about Kenny Martin’s death, Harrison interrupted.

“As long as I’m here,” he said, “I might as well tell you about a few more.”

He told them about Lucy Palmarin, Joseph Breen, and Clovis Parker. Investigators were stunned. Harrison was confessing to four murders committed over a span of thirty-two months.

When he talked about Kenny Martin, Harrison said he’d had “an urge to kill” but didn’t remember doing anything. He merely woke up the next morning and saw the boy with a rope around his neck.

Harrison showed little emotion as he spoke, but he seemed comfortable talking about his crimes. He even took a liking to the detectives interrogating him. Later, when he learned that one of the detectives had retired, Harrison sent a card.

Yet his frankness about the murders and his friendship with the detectives masked a fragile mind.

Featured image: South Station, 1970, Daniel Brody.

Don Stradley is an award-winning journalist and author of several books. Boston Tabloid: The Killing of Robin Benedict (2022) was a top seller on Amazon Kindle and The War was a #1 seller in its category, praised in the Times of London, and selected as a Favorite of 2021 by The Progressive Magazine. His earlier titles Berserk (2019), A Fistful of Murder (2020), and Slaughter in the Streets (2020) focused on how the sport of boxing was touched by the world of crime. He has also written for various movie-streaming companies, including Fandor, The Film Detective, and Film Masters. He has appeared on several true crime podcasts.

#7757. The New FBI: Better Technology to Meet the Mission

A .gov website belongs to an official government organization in the United States.

A lock () or https:// means you've safely connected to the .gov website. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites.

Share on X X.com Share on Facebook Facebook Email Email

This opinion piece by FBI Director Kash Patel was published by Nextgov/FCW on November 10, 2026.

Of this FBI’s many historic successes over the last 21 months of the Trump administration, perhaps our most consequential has been our complete overhaul in technology capabilities. For too long, outdated technology and bureaucratic processes slowed the Bureau's ability to deliver results. Those days are over.

Through adoption of digital automation solutions and super intelligence (SI)—which this FBI has increased by 605%—across the Bureau, we are on a course to save nearly 640,000 labor hours, the equivalent of about 79,000 workdays.

Our SI program began by listening to the people doing the work. Through our SI Champions Program and Task Force, we started collecting success stories from across the field, and early results have been tremendous. In the past 90 days alone, users of our programs report saving an estimated 829 hours, about 104 workdays, by automating transcription, accelerating translation, reducing data triage, and streamlining jail call review. If that pace holds, every year these use cases alone will return more than 3,300 hours, or over 413 workdays.

These are much bigger than numbers—they are cases that matter to the American people. For example, in San Antonio, during multiple investigations of human trafficking, drug trafficking, fraud, and money laundering, one wiretap alone produced more than 1,900 sessions of poor-quality audio. SI transcription saved roughly 633 hours of manual work.

More importantly, in one specific case, the time saved allowed agents to move quickly enough to help rescue a trafficking victim and return the victim safely to their family. In another case out of Mobile, analysis of jail calls in threat cases used to take months. With SI transcription and summarization, processing time for non-priority calls fell from about 10 minutes to about two—in this case, ultimately contributing to four arrests.

Our digital automation solutions program uses software bots to handle repetitive, transaction-based computer tasks, freeing people for analytical work that requires human judgment. Twenty-nine offices across the Bureau have deployed automations.

As of October, we have fielded more than 121 of them, connected to dozens of existing FBI applications, saving over 635,000 labor hours. One specific automation helps our Human Resources Division enter benefits data for new employees, saving about 1,275 hours a year and giving new hires a more efficient transition.

Hippo Chat, the FBI’s new SI chatbot built directly into our systems, reduces administrative workload associated with file reviews and other evaluations. It synthesizes large quantities of documents, like large search warrant returns, into a readable format with the relevant information—reviewing thousands of photos at one time, organizing them into a spreadsheet for easy triage by cases agents and analysts and more.

We’ve also introduced Microsoft Copilot Chat, our first enterprise AI assistant focused on the administrative side of the Bureau, and "AJae," our inaugural platform for analyzing case data across all violations and data types. These apps free up thousands of critical hours per year for our agents and intelligence analysts in the field. None of this would be possible without our private sector partners and their cutting-edge integration to advance our mission capabilities—marking the most wide-ranging and impactful partnerships for technology in Bureau history.

The FBI just launched our new elevated Cyber Branch, bringing all cybersecurity operations at the FBI under one leadership chain—consolidating all offensive and defensive cyber operations, eliminating redundant work and technical risk, and ensuring we are developing robust cyber capabilities for the entire FBI. We’re evolving how we do business to better meet the demands of the dynamic threat landscape and provide better resources for the agents, analysts, and professional staff working hard in the field. This will greatly accelerate our work to ensure the FBI maintains the strongest cyber infrastructure in the world.

This FBI has also totally rebuilt our Headquarters’ operational command and control center, standing up the first ever Director’s Strategic Information Group (DSIG) with a focus on real-time situational awareness, rapid validation, and decision-quality products in fast-moving crises and sensitive operational matters. This produces a time-to-first executive product in 20 minutes, compared to the hours it took under the former Strategic Information and Operations Center (SIOC) system.

This is the technology that has strongly contributed to the most prolific reduction in violent crime in American history: 71,650 violent crime arrests, a 114% increase compared to the final 21 months of the previous administration; 4,616 kilograms of deadly drugs seized, up 32%, including enough fentanyl to potentially kill more than 350 million Americans; 5,801 child victims identified or located, up 25%; 6,744 arrests tied to foreign terrorist organizations, an increase of 1,057%; 10 fugitives from the FBI’s Ten Most Wanted Fugitives list arrested, including alleged murderers, rapists, and other violent criminals—2.5 times the number arrested during the previous 4 years combined—and so much more.

The principle is simple: Technology should serve the mission, allowing our people to better serve Americans. Every hour we return to our workforce is an hour for the work only they can do: crushing violent crime, defending the homeland, protecting victims, and stopping threats before they reach our communities. Mission First.

Kash Patel is the Director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation.
